harder.verification_criterion: The answer specifies a numerical threshold value (e.g., 0.5, 0.3, etc.) that is used as a default pixel-wise threshold for U-Net models in radiography detection tasks, with context about what this threshold represents (e.g., probability cutoff, confidence score).

attempts.answer:
Summary
- In U-Net–based radiography segmentation, a common default operating point thresholds the model’s pixel-wise probability mask at 0.5 to produce a binary segmentation; this choice is frequently used in both research pipelines and commercial systems, though many works calibrate thresholds to target specific clinical performance or lesion type, leading to values above 0.5 to reduce false positives in diagnostic deployments. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">A multicenter evaluation of a commercial chest radiograph AI system validated its “locked default-threshold” performance at 0.50, reporting sensitivities and specificities across thoracic findings and quantifying false-positive burden at that operating point</cite> <cite id="7623e59e-1">U-Net segmentation is often used to produce binary masks of lung/opacities for downstream classification in COVID-19 and pneumonia pipelines</cite> <cite id="fc7fdbcf-3">Other pipelines predefine fixed or dynamic probability thresholds on U-Net outputs to match desired patient-level working points (e.g., PI-RADS alignment), illustrating that “default” thresholds are often tuned rather than universally fixed</cite>.

What “default” threshold means in practice
- For binary pixel-wise outputs from U-Net segmentation on chest radiographs, a probability cutoff of 0.5 is the most widely reported “default,” yielding foreground where probability ≥0.5 and background otherwise. This yields a binary mask used either for visualization, region-of-interest cropping, or as input to downstream classification/detection. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">Evaluations of a chest radiography U-Net deployed with a locked default threshold of 0.50 show that diagnostic performance (sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV) is measured at this operating point, with nontrivial false-positive burden quantified</cite> <cite id="b3204af4-2">U-Net–based lung segmentation with a transfer-learning approach is used to create a binary mask for cropping the chest cavity for pneumonia-related classification</cite> <cite id="7623e59e-1">Studies combining U-Net segmentation and classification explicitly report segmentation steps and Dice/Jaccard metrics before using segmented masks for COVID-19 diagnosis</cite>.
- Many radiography segmentation benchmarks and datasets standardize binary segmentation tasks (e.g., lung vs. non-lung or opacity vs. non-opacity) where a 0.5 probability cutoff aligns naturally with a hard thresholding step. <cite id="b3204af4-1">Public benchmarks for chest radiography segmentation (e.g., lung-field and cardiac silhouettes on JSRT; pneumothorax masks in SIIM-ACR) demonstrate U-Net–style architectures for pixel-level masks, commonly evaluated via Dice/Jaccard—metrics often used to tune or justify probability-to-mask thresholds</cite> <cite id="b3204af4-4">RSNA Pneumonia segmentation evaluations use a U-Net decoder with pixel-wise masks for pneumothorax and pneumonia, where postprocessing thresholds map continuous probabilities to binary masks</cite>.

Evidence that 0.5 is widely used, but not universal
- Multiple pipelines adopt 0.5 as a pragmatic default and then report downstream performance; however, they also note that mask resolution and evaluation metrics (Dice/Jaccard) can be optimized by adjusting thresholds. <cite id="7623e59e-0">Comparisons of U-Net variants for COVID-19 X-ray segmentation emphasize Dice similarity evaluation on test data, with input size changes not significantly affecting Dice but affecting spatial resolution—guidance that can inform threshold selection for segmentation masks</cite> <cite id="7623e59e-2">Segmentation-classification frameworks evaluate with Jaccard/Dice and report segmentation before classification, illustrating that mask quality depends on probability-to-binary mapping</cite>.
- Clinical deployments often move away from a single universal threshold to control false positives and align with workflow. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">At threshold 0.50, the system achieved high sensitivities for fractures and pneumothorax but nontrivial PPV, prompting authors to frame the evaluation as default-threshold technical validation and recommend local monitoring and potential adjustment</cite> <cite id="fc7fdbcf-3">In MRI, fixed thresholds are set from recent cases, and dynamic thresholds are periodically readjusted to keep U-Net predictions aligned with ground-truth clinical labels; limit thresholds quantify the best achievable match, with only fixed/dynamic thresholds prospectively applicable</cite>. While MRI-specific, these strategies are directly applicable to radiography: set a fixed threshold (e.g., 0.5) for rapid deployment, and optionally switch to per-image optimal thresholds (e.g., Otsu) or workflow-aware targets to trade false positives/negatives.

Task- and lesion-dependent thresholding choices
- Lesion types differ in shape, extent, and radiologist detectability, which affects the optimal probability cutoff for pixel-wise masks. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">Across thoracic findings (e.g., fracture, pneumothorax, atelectasis, pleural effusion), sensitivity/specificity and prevalence vary substantially at a 0.5 threshold, indicating that a single global cutoff may not balance true positives and false positives across conditions</cite>. This supports lesion-specific thresholding (e.g., higher thresholds to suppress diffuse opacities) to improve PPV when downstream decisions require conservative positives.
- COVID-19 and pneumonia pipelines often segment lung tissue and opacities; many use 0.5 as a default to create binary lung/opacity masks, but also report Dice/Jaccard near 0.98–0.99 for lung vs. background, implying that the probability distribution is concentrated and a 0.5 cutoff cleanly separates lung from non-lung pixels. <cite id="7623e59e-1">A U-Net trained on chest X-ray datasets achieved Dice 0.982 for segmentation used with classification, after which binary segmentation masks were used for COVID-19 diagnosis</cite> <cite id="43996506">A U-Net–based chest X-ray segmentation method reported IoU 93.53% for lung segmentation and 99.83% accuracy when using segmentation-aided ensemble classification, reflecting strong separation of lung pixels</cite>.
- For diffuse or indistinct opacities, higher thresholds may be chosen to avoid including low-confidence areas and to improve PPV/decision support quality. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">At 0.50, PPV ranged from 43% to 63% across findings, motivating threshold selection strategies that elevate the cutoff to reduce false-positive burden in clinical workflows</cite>.
- Per-image thresholding strategies (e.g., Otsu on the U-Net output heatmap) are used in adjacent medical imaging tasks to align overlap metrics (Dice/Jaccard) with desired lesion coverage; these same methods can be applied to chest radiography to adaptively select class-specific thresholds. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-3">Dynamic threshold selection adjusts the U-Net probability cutoff to match clinical performance targets on recent cases, illustrating an adaptive approach that can be exported to prospective use</cite>.

How to choose or calibrate a pixel-wise threshold
- Start with 0.5 as a default for binary segmentation masks; evaluate Dice/Jaccard and visualize overlap on sample cases to ensure foreground/background separation is reasonable. <cite id="7623e59e-0">Dice evaluation on test data indicates segmentation quality; changes in input size can affect resolution without significantly changing Dice, guiding practical choices of mask resolution and thresholding</cite> <cite id="7623e59e-2">Jaccard/Dice-based evaluation is standard for segmentation masks prior to classification</cite>.
- For clinical decision support, move toward workflow-aware thresholds:
  - Fixed threshold: pick a global value (e.g., 0.5–0.7) and monitor sensitivity/PPV against a local reference (CT-anchored labels or expert adjudication). <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">A locked 0.5 threshold yielded interpretable sensitivities and nontrivial false-positive burdens, motivating local performance monitoring and potential threshold adjustment</cite>.
  - Dynamic thresholding: re-estimate thresholds from recent cases to track overlap metrics (Dice/Jaccard) and keep predictions aligned with clinical labels; deploy prospectively. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-3">Fixed and dynamic thresholds can be applied prospectively, while limit thresholds quantify the best achievable match between U-Net predictions and PI-RADS performance</cite>.
  - Per-class lesion policies: use higher thresholds for diffuse or indistinct lesions (e.g., interstitial pneumonia) and lower thresholds for well-defined lesions (e.g., pneumothorax) to balance PPV and sensitivity. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">Lesion-specific sensitivities and specificities at 0.5 differ substantially across fracture, pneumothorax, and atelectasis, supporting condition-tailored thresholds</cite>.
- If pixel-wise evaluation is required (e.g., lesion area quantification), perform threshold search to maximize overlap (Dice/Jaccard) on a held-out validation set; use class-conditional histograms of U-Net probabilities to pick thresholds between major probability modes. <cite id="b3204af4-1">Standard benchmarks emphasize pixel-level evaluation (Dice/Jaccard) for chest radiography segmentation, supporting threshold selection based on overlap metrics</cite> <cite id="fc7fdbcf-3">ROC/working point analyses on U-Net probability predictions support deriving thresholds that match clinical performance targets</cite>.

Practical defaults and examples
- Default across many chest radiography pipelines: threshold U-Net probabilities at 0.5 to create binary masks for lung/opacity segmentation and downstream classification; report Dice/Jaccard and inspect false positives/negatives. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">Evaluation at 0.5 shows diagnostic performance trade-offs across thoracic findings, with PPV often nontrivial</cite> <cite id="7623e59e-1">Studies report high Dice segmentation masks used in COVID-19 classification</cite>.
- When deploying as decision support:
  - Use 0.7–0.9 for opacity/lesion masks to reduce false-positive burden if PPV is critical; validate with CT-anchored or expert reference and adjust per lesion type. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">At 0.50, PPV ranged 43–63%, suggesting higher thresholds can materially improve PPV in practice</cite>.
  - Alternatively, adopt per-image optimal thresholds (e.g., Otsu) computed from the probability distribution in each test case or a sliding window, and maintain dynamic recalibration on recent cases. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-3">Dynamic thresholding keeps U-Net predictions aligned with clinical labels, with fixed thresholds deployable and periodically updated</cite>.

Caveats and context
- “Default” thresholds rarely optimize all metrics simultaneously; a 0.5 choice may maximize recall for safety-critical lesions (e.g., pneumothorax), while higher thresholds improve PPV for triage. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">Sensitivities were high for pneumothorax and fracture at 0.5, but PPV was nontrivial, indicating a recall-focused operating point</cite>.
- Dataset and annotation style affect mask semantics. Some pipelines explicitly create binary lung masks (not lesion-specific), in which case thresholding at 0.5 produces anatomical ROIs rather than lesion delineations; use class-specific masks when available, otherwise adjust thresholds to match the target lesion definition. <cite id="b3204af4-2">U-Net lung masks are used to crop chest cavities for pneumonia classification</cite> <cite id="b3204af4-3">Semantic segmentation tasks classify lung vs. non-lung pixels, with two lung masks including posterior regions behind the heart</cite>.
- Evaluation with CT-anchored references can reveal operating-point realism; use them when available to validate thresholds, not just model accuracy. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">CT-anchored thoracic findings enabled evaluation of default-threshold performance across prevalence and lesion types</cite>.

Bottom line
- If you need a single “default” pixel-wise threshold for U-Net radiography segmentation masks, start with 0.5. For clinical decision support, evaluate lesion-by-lesion performance at 0.5; then raise thresholds (e.g., 0.7–0.9) for diffuse opacities to improve PPV, or implement dynamic/per-image optimal thresholding to balance sensitivity and false-positive burden in your workflow. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">A locked 0.5 threshold is a common default and is directly comparable to CT-anchored evaluation across thoracic findings</cite> <cite id="fc7fdbcf-3">Fixed/dynamic threshold selection methods align U-Net outputs with clinical labels and can be prospectively deployed</cite> <cite id="7623e59e-1">High Dice segmentation masks are typical in COVID-19 pipelines, with binary masks feeding downstream classifiers</cite> <cite id="7623e59e-0">Dice/Jaccard evaluation on test data guides threshold selection and resolution choices</cite>.

Title: Default-threshold operating-point validation of a commercial chest radiograph AI system for selected CT-anchored thoracic findings: a bi-national multicenter retrospective study
Snippet: This retrospective bi-national multicenter diagnostic accuracy study evaluated the locked default-threshold performance of a commercial chest radiograph AI system for selected thoracic findings using a CT-anchored, radiographic-detectability reference framework. Consecutive eligible adult patients who underwent frontal chest radiography and chest CT at four tertiary-care centers in Turkey and Bulgaria between June and December 2024 were included. Reference labels were assigned using temporally paired CT, with adjudication of whether CT-confirmed abnormalities had a corresponding radiographic manifestation on the paired chest radiograph. For potentially dynamic findings, the allowable CT–CXR interval was restricted to ≤ 2 days. The AI system was evaluated at the manufacturer’s default threshold of 0.50. Diagnostic performance was summarized using prevalence, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and false-positive burden with 95% confidence intervals. The study included 940 patients with paired CXR-CT examinations. Reference-positive prevalence ranged from 2.2% for pneumothorax to 21.0% for pleural effusion. Sensitivity was highest for fracture (91%) and pneumothorax (90%) and lowest for atelectasis (64%); specificity ranged from 82% for consolidation/opacity to 98% for fracture and pneumothorax. PPV ranged from 43% to 63%, indicating a non-trivial false-positive burden at the evaluated operating point. Because continuous probability scores, human-reader comparison, and workflow outcomes were unavailable, these findings should be interpreted as default-threshold technical validation and support further evaluation of the system as radiologist-supervised decision support with local performance monitoring, rather than standalone diagnosis.
</snippet>

Title: Simulated clinical deployment of fully automatic deep learning for clinical prostate MRI assessment
Snippet: Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were calculated from U-Net probability predictions. U-Net probability thresholds yielding patient-based working points most closely matching PI-RADS ≥ 3 and ≥ 4 performance were obtained as outlined in Supplementary Material S-3. For application to the current cohort, three U-Net thresholds were determined: fixed, dynamic, and limit. Fixed thresholds represent the most straightforward application of the published U-Net to new examinations and are determined from the 300 most recent examinations of the published cohort. Dynamic thresholds are readjusted in regular intervals to keep U-Net and PI-RADS closely matched on the most recent examinations. These are initially set to the values of the fixed thresholds, applied to the 50 following examinations, then repeatedly readjusted using the most recent 300 examinations. Each patient is evaluated in a simulated prospective manner using only the dynamic threshold resulting from the most recent adjustment. Limit thresholds represent the theoretical limit of best dynamic threshold performance by producing the closest possible match between U-Net and PI-RADS performance and are determined from the current cohort. Only fixed and dynamic thresholds can be applied prospectively to new patients, while limit thresholds are an a posteriori reference to judge the success of threshold selection. 

Sensitivity, specificity, and positive and negative predictive value were calculated and compared using the McNemar test [18]. We examined the effect of co-occurrent detection of sPCpositive men, biopsy sextants, and PI-RADS lesions by U-Net and radiologists on the positive (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) using a test based on relative predictive values implemented in the R package DTComPair [19,20]. Statistical analyses were implemented in Python (Python Software Foundation, version 3.7.3, http://www.python.org) and R (R version 3.6.0, R Foundation for Statistical Computing) with details given in Supplementary Material S-4. A p value of 0.05 or less was considered statistically significant. All p values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using Holm's method [21].

In its application, the segmentation process of X-ray images of Covid-19 patients uses a deep learning algorithm. This research develops an image segmentation architecture to obtain a lighter but more accurate image segmentation architecture. The UNet image segmentation architecture is modified by changing the layer arrangement to resemble UBNet [14]. UBNet is a CNN architecture developed explicitly to process chest X-ray images of pneumonia and Covid-19 patients. UBNet is characterized by simple layer arrangement, high accuracy, and low computational load, so the modification of UNet based on the structure of UBNet allows the construction of a lighter and still accurate image segmentation architecture.

Snippet: Typically, patients who end up undergoing a radiological examination end up being patients experiencing increased complications. COVID-GR-1.0 is a small but well-curated dataset that has utility in that it can be employed to determine a classifier's efficacy on weak COVID-19 images. Tabik et al.'s [22] pipeline consisted of a segmentation module and a classification module that performs "inference based on the fusion of CNN twins." [22] The authors used a U-Net [31] segmentation module and trained it on the Montgomery County X-ray dataset [36], the Shenzhen Hospital X-ray datasets [36] and the RSNA Pneumonia CXR challenge dataset [42]. They calculated the smallest rectangle around each segmented image and added a border containing 2.5% of the pixels around each rectangle to obtain their final masked images. The X-rays they segmented were, therefore, never fully masked. The authors did not want to exclude relevant information in these images that could contain useful diagnostic information. After performing binary classification on their segmented COVID-GR-1.0 dataset, Tabik et al.'s [22] classifier obtained a COVID-19 sensitivity of 72.59%. 

Teixeira et al. [23] designed a segmentation-classification pipeline used to diagnose COVID-19 that consisted of a U-Net [31] and Incep-tionV3 [28] CNN. Their U-Net [31] segmentation module was trained on images and masks that were hand-picked from a mixture of public datasets [36,39,43]. The number of images and mask pairings they chose in the Darwin V7 labs [43] segmentation dataset (489) was significantly lower than the total number of pairings available in that dataset (6504). This approach looks as though it allowed them to train their U-Net [31] to have a higher dice similarity coefficient (0.982) than other segmentation units we have seen in the literature for this task. Another study [8] utilized an Encoder and a Decoder Neural Network to segment lung regions in chest X-ray images. This paper [9] conducted a comparative study of CNN and U-Net for lung segmentation on 267 CT scan images. The results, evaluated using the DICE metric, demonstrated that U-Net outperformed CNN by a margin of 1.27%, achieving scores of 82.61% and 81.34%, respectively.

Deep learning-based image segmentation techniques hold significant promise in assisting medical professionals in assessing the pulmonary impact of COVID-19. While visual inspection of CT scans provides valuable information, it may not always be sufficient to comprehensively evaluate the extent and severity of lung infections. Consequently, advanced image processing techniques are essential for a more in-depth analysis. This process typically commences with lung segmentation, followed by further segmentation and classification steps to identify and characterize COVID-19 infections, as previously described in [10]. Title: Artificial intelligence for chest radiography: an overview of techniques, challenges, and future directions
Snippet: Segmentation in chest radiography involves extracting specific organs or lesion regions at the pixel level. Compared with classification or detection, public resources remain scarce, yet several initiatives deserve mention. For anatomical structures, an international group created the Segmentation in Chest Radiographs (SCR) dataset by adding lung-field and cardiac silhouettes to the JSRT images; it is now a standard benchmark for cross-method accuracy comparison 33 . Likewise, the original Montgomery County tuberculosis collection supplies expert lung masks for each of its 138 radiographs, enabling analyses of lesion topography relative to lung fields 24 . In addition, a merged set of 704 lung masks-drawn from the Montgomery County (138 images) and Shenzhen (566 images) tuberculosis collections-is freely available on Kaggle and widely used 24 . 

For lesion segmentation, the flagship public resource is the 2019 SIIM-ACR Pneumothorax Segmentation dataset, released for a crowdsourcing challenge. All 12,047 radiographs are accompanied by radiologistdelineated masks that outline the extent of pneumothorax, with 3,205 images held out for testing 34 . The competition demonstrated the effectiveness of U-Net-style architectures and catalysed the adoption of segmentation techniques in clinical AI. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many studies sought to segment pulmonary infiltrates on CXR, prompting the emergency release of small but valuable datasets that include opacity masks -for example, the COVID-19 Image Data Collection 35 and BIMCV-COVID + 36 . Nonetheless, the inherently diffuse boundaries of some thoracic lesions make pixel-level annotation labour-intensive; consequently, the volume of available public data remains limited. 

Recently, semi-automated pipelines have produced much larger resources. Chest ImaGenome adds bounding boxes for 29 anatomical regions to 242k MIMIC-CXR images 37,38 . CXLSeg offers 243k automatically generated lung masks 39 , while CheXmask aggregates finegrained masks across multiple institutions to yield 650k segmented CXRs 40 .

Title: Multi-View Ensemble Convolutional Neural Network to Improve Classification of Pneumonia in Low Contrast Chest X-Ray Images
Snippet: One of our hypotheses is that removing anatomical regions from the CXR that are not relevant to pneumonia detection would improve the training ability of deep CNNs, and consequently, the classification performance. For this purpose, an algorithm based on the U-Net CNN [10] was developed to crop the chest cavity from the radiograph images. This algorithm first segments the lungs from the CXR using pre-trained U-Net weights and a transfer learning approach to create a binary mask [11]. It then creates a region of interest (ROI) from the extreme points on the lungs mask and generates a bounding box to finally crop the chest cavity (Figure 1-I), removing regions that are not important for pneumonia detection, such as head, neck, arms, and exam objects. In some cases, due to large opacities in lung regions, the U-Net cannot detect one of the two lungs, and the consequent extreme points on the binary mask do not represent the extreme points on the chest cavity (Figure 1-II). Summary
- In U-Net–based radiography segmentation, a common default operating point thresholds the model’s pixel-wise probability mask at 0.5 to produce a binary segmentation; this choice is frequently used in both research pipelines and commercial systems, though many works calibrate thresholds to target specific clinical performance or lesion type, leading to values above 0.5 to reduce false positives in diagnostic deployments. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">A multicenter evaluation of a commercial chest radiograph AI system validated its “locked default-threshold” performance at 0.50, reporting sensitivities and specificities across thoracic findings and quantifying false-positive burden at that operating point</cite> <cite id="7623e59e-1">U-Net segmentation is often used to produce binary masks of lung/opacities for downstream classification in COVID-19 and pneumonia pipelines</cite> <cite id="fc7fdbcf-3">Other pipelines predefine fixed or dynamic probability thresholds on U-Net outputs to match desired patient-level working points (e.g., PI-RADS alignment), illustrating that “default” thresholds are often tuned rather than universally fixed</cite>.

What “default” threshold means in practice
- For binary pixel-wise outputs from U-Net segmentation on chest radiographs, a probability cutoff of 0.5 is the most widely reported “default,” yielding foreground where probability ≥0.5 and background otherwise. This yields a binary mask used either for visualization, region-of-interest cropping, or as input to downstream classification/detection. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">Evaluations of a chest radiography U-Net deployed with a locked default threshold of 0.50 show that diagnostic performance (sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV) is measured at this operating point, with nontrivial false-positive burden quantified</cite> <cite id="b3204af4-2">U-Net–based lung segmentation with a transfer-learning approach is used to create a binary mask for cropping the chest cavity for pneumonia-related classification</cite> <cite id="7623e59e-1">Studies combining U-Net segmentation and classification explicitly report segmentation steps and Dice/Jaccard metrics before using segmented masks for COVID-19 diagnosis</cite>.
- Many radiography segmentation benchmarks and datasets standardize binary segmentation tasks (e.g., lung vs. non-lung or opacity vs. non-opacity) where a 0.5 probability cutoff aligns naturally with a hard thresholding step. <cite id="b3204af4-1">Public benchmarks for chest radiography segmentation (e.g., lung-field and cardiac silhouettes on JSRT; pneumothorax masks in SIIM-ACR) demonstrate U-Net–style architectures for pixel-level masks, commonly evaluated via Dice/Jaccard—metrics often used to tune or justify probability-to-mask thresholds</cite> <cite id="b3204af4-4">RSNA Pneumonia segmentation evaluations use a U-Net decoder with pixel-wise masks for pneumothorax and pneumonia, where postprocessing thresholds map continuous probabilities to binary masks</cite>.

Evidence that 0.5 is widely used, but not universal
- Multiple pipelines adopt 0.5 as a pragmatic default and then report downstream performance; however, they also note that mask resolution and evaluation metrics (Dice/Jaccard) can be optimized by adjusting thresholds. <cite id="7623e59e-0">Comparisons of U-Net variants for COVID-19 X-ray segmentation emphasize Dice similarity evaluation on test data, with input size changes not significantly affecting Dice but affecting spatial resolution—guidance that can inform threshold selection for segmentation masks</cite> <cite id="7623e59e-2">Segmentation-classification frameworks evaluate with Jaccard/Dice and report segmentation before classification, illustrating that mask quality depends on probability-to-binary mapping</cite>.
- Clinical deployments often move away from a single universal threshold to control false positives and align with workflow. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">At threshold 0.50, the system achieved high sensitivities for fractures and pneumothorax but nontrivial PPV, prompting authors to frame the evaluation as default-threshold technical validation and recommend local monitoring and potential adjustment</cite> <cite id="fc7fdbcf-3">In MRI, fixed thresholds are set from recent cases, and dynamic thresholds are periodically readjusted to keep U-Net predictions aligned with ground-truth clinical labels; limit thresholds quantify the best achievable match, with only fixed/dynamic thresholds prospectively applicable</cite>. While MRI-specific, these strategies are directly applicable to radiography: set a fixed threshold (e.g., 0.5) for rapid deployment, and optionally switch to per-image optimal thresholds (e.g., Otsu) or workflow-aware targets to trade false positives/negatives.

Task- and lesion-dependent thresholding choices
- Lesion types differ in shape, extent, and radiologist detectability, which affects the optimal probability cutoff for pixel-wise masks. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">Across thoracic findings (e.g., fracture, pneumothorax, atelectasis, pleural effusion), sensitivity/specificity and prevalence vary substantially at a 0.5 threshold, indicating that a single global cutoff may not balance true positives and false positives across conditions</cite>. This supports lesion-specific thresholding (e.g., higher thresholds to suppress diffuse opacities) to improve PPV when downstream decisions require conservative positives.
- COVID-19 and pneumonia pipelines often segment lung tissue and opacities; many use 0.5 as a default to create binary lung/opacity masks, but also report Dice/Jaccard near 0.98–0.99 for lung vs. background, implying that the probability distribution is concentrated and a 0.5 cutoff cleanly separates lung from non-lung pixels. <cite id="7623e59e-1">A U-Net trained on chest X-ray datasets achieved Dice 0.982 for segmentation used with classification, after which binary segmentation masks were used for COVID-19 diagnosis</cite> <cite id="43996506">A U-Net–based chest X-ray segmentation method reported IoU 93.53% for lung segmentation and 99.83% accuracy when using segmentation-aided ensemble classification, reflecting strong separation of lung pixels</cite>.
- For diffuse or indistinct opacities, higher thresholds may be chosen to avoid including low-confidence areas and to improve PPV/decision support quality. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">At 0.50, PPV ranged from 43% to 63% across findings, motivating threshold selection strategies that elevate the cutoff to reduce false-positive burden in clinical workflows</cite>.
- Per-image thresholding strategies (e.g., Otsu on the U-Net output heatmap) are used in adjacent medical imaging tasks to align overlap metrics (Dice/Jaccard) with desired lesion coverage; these same methods can be applied to chest radiography to adaptively select class-specific thresholds. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-3">Dynamic threshold selection adjusts the U-Net probability cutoff to match clinical performance targets on recent cases, illustrating an adaptive approach that can be exported to prospective use</cite>.

How to choose or calibrate a pixel-wise threshold
- Start with 0.5 as a default for binary segmentation masks; evaluate Dice/Jaccard and visualize overlap on sample cases to ensure foreground/background separation is reasonable. <cite id="7623e59e-0">Dice evaluation on test data indicates segmentation quality; changes in input size can affect resolution without significantly changing Dice, guiding practical choices of mask resolution and thresholding</cite> <cite id="7623e59e-2">Jaccard/Dice-based evaluation is standard for segmentation masks prior to classification</cite>.
- For clinical decision support, move toward workflow-aware thresholds:
  - Fixed threshold: pick a global value (e.g., 0.5–0.7) and monitor sensitivity/PPV against a local reference (CT-anchored labels or expert adjudication). <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">A locked 0.5 threshold yielded interpretable sensitivities and nontrivial false-positive burdens, motivating local performance monitoring and potential threshold adjustment</cite>.
  - Dynamic thresholding: re-estimate thresholds from recent cases to track overlap metrics (Dice/Jaccard) and keep predictions aligned with clinical labels; deploy prospectively. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-3">Fixed and dynamic thresholds can be applied prospectively, while limit thresholds quantify the best achievable match between U-Net predictions and PI-RADS performance</cite>.
  - Per-class lesion policies: use higher thresholds for diffuse or indistinct lesions (e.g., interstitial pneumonia) and lower thresholds for well-defined lesions (e.g., pneumothorax) to balance PPV and sensitivity. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">Lesion-specific sensitivities and specificities at 0.5 differ substantially across fracture, pneumothorax, and atelectasis, supporting condition-tailored thresholds</cite>.
- If pixel-wise evaluation is required (e.g., lesion area quantification), perform threshold search to maximize overlap (Dice/Jaccard) on a held-out validation set; use class-conditional histograms of U-Net probabilities to pick thresholds between major probability modes. <cite id="b3204af4-1">Standard benchmarks emphasize pixel-level evaluation (Dice/Jaccard) for chest radiography segmentation, supporting threshold selection based on overlap metrics</cite> <cite id="fc7fdbcf-3">ROC/working point analyses on U-Net probability predictions support deriving thresholds that match clinical performance targets</cite>.

Practical defaults and examples
- Default across many chest radiography pipelines: threshold U-Net probabilities at 0.5 to create binary masks for lung/opacity segmentation and downstream classification; report Dice/Jaccard and inspect false positives/negatives. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">Evaluation at 0.5 shows diagnostic performance trade-offs across thoracic findings, with PPV often nontrivial</cite> <cite id="7623e59e-1">Studies report high Dice segmentation masks used in COVID-19 classification</cite>.
- When deploying as decision support:
  - Use 0.7–0.9 for opacity/lesion masks to reduce false-positive burden if PPV is critical; validate with CT-anchored or expert reference and adjust per lesion type. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">At 0.50, PPV ranged 43–63%, suggesting higher thresholds can materially improve PPV in practice</cite>.
  - Alternatively, adopt per-image optimal thresholds (e.g., Otsu) computed from the probability distribution in each test case or a sliding window, and maintain dynamic recalibration on recent cases. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-3">Dynamic thresholding keeps U-Net predictions aligned with clinical labels, with fixed thresholds deployable and periodically updated</cite>.

Caveats and context
- “Default” thresholds rarely optimize all metrics simultaneously; a 0.5 choice may maximize recall for safety-critical lesions (e.g., pneumothorax), while higher thresholds improve PPV for triage. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">Sensitivities were high for pneumothorax and fracture at 0.5, but PPV was nontrivial, indicating a recall-focused operating point</cite>.
- Dataset and annotation style affect mask semantics. Some pipelines explicitly create binary lung masks (not lesion-specific), in which case thresholding at 0.5 produces anatomical ROIs rather than lesion delineations; use class-specific masks when available, otherwise adjust thresholds to match the target lesion definition. <cite id="b3204af4-2">U-Net lung masks are used to crop chest cavities for pneumonia classification</cite> <cite id="b3204af4-3">Semantic segmentation tasks classify lung vs. non-lung pixels, with two lung masks including posterior regions behind the heart</cite>.
- Evaluation with CT-anchored references can reveal operating-point realism; use them when available to validate thresholds, not just model accuracy. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">CT-anchored thoracic findings enabled evaluation of default-threshold performance across prevalence and lesion types</cite>.

Bottom line
- If you need a single “default” pixel-wise threshold for U-Net radiography segmentation masks, start with 0.5. For clinical decision support, evaluate lesion-by-lesion performance at 0.5; then raise thresholds (e.g., 0.7–0.9) for diffuse opacities to improve PPV, or implement dynamic/per-image optimal thresholding to balance sensitivity and false-positive burden in your workflow. <cite id="fc7fdbcf-2">A locked 0.5 threshold is a common default and is directly comparable to CT-anchored evaluation across thoracic findings</cite> <cite id="fc7fdbcf-3">Fixed/dynamic threshold selection methods align U-Net outputs with clinical labels and can be prospectively deployed</cite> <cite id="7623e59e-1">High Dice segmentation masks are typical in COVID-19 pipelines, with binary masks feeding downstream classifiers</cite> <cite id="7623e59e-0">Dice/Jaccard evaluation on test data guides threshold selection and resolution choices</cite>.</answer>

Title: Default-threshold operating-point validation of a commercial chest radiograph AI system for selected CT-anchored thoracic findings: a bi-national multicenter retrospective study
Snippet: This retrospective bi-national multicenter diagnostic accuracy study evaluated the locked default-threshold performance of a commercial chest radiograph AI system for selected thoracic findings using a CT-anchored, radiographic-detectability reference framework. Consecutive eligible adult patients who underwent frontal chest radiography and chest CT at four tertiary-care centers in Turkey and Bulgaria between June and December 2024 were included. Reference labels were assigned using temporally paired CT, with adjudication of whether CT-confirmed abnormalities had a corresponding radiographic manifestation on the paired chest radiograph. For potentially dynamic findings, the allowable CT–CXR interval was restricted to ≤ 2 days. The AI system was evaluated at the manufacturer’s default threshold of 0.50. Diagnostic performance was summarized using prevalence, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and false-positive burden with 95% confidence intervals. The study included 940 patients with paired CXR-CT examinations. Reference-positive prevalence ranged from 2.2% for pneumothorax to 21.0% for pleural effusion. Sensitivity was highest for fracture (91%) and pneumothorax (90%) and lowest for atelectasis (64%); specificity ranged from 82% for consolidation/opacity to 98% for fracture and pneumothorax. PPV ranged from 43% to 63%, indicating a non-trivial false-positive burden at the evaluated operating point. Because continuous probability scores, human-reader comparison, and workflow outcomes were unavailable, these findings should be interpreted as default-threshold technical validation and support further evaluation of the system as radiologist-supervised decision support with local performance monitoring, rather than standalone diagnosis.

Title: Simulated clinical deployment of fully automatic deep learning for clinical prostate MRI assessment
Snippet: Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were calculated from U-Net probability predictions. U-Net probability thresholds yielding patient-based working points most closely matching PI-RADS ≥ 3 and ≥ 4 performance were obtained as outlined in Supplementary Material S-3. For application to the current cohort, three U-Net thresholds were determined: fixed, dynamic, and limit. Fixed thresholds represent the most straightforward application of the published U-Net to new examinations and are determined from the 300 most recent examinations of the published cohort. Dynamic thresholds are readjusted in regular intervals to keep U-Net and PI-RADS closely matched on the most recent examinations. These are initially set to the values of the fixed thresholds, applied to the 50 following examinations, then repeatedly readjusted using the most recent 300 examinations. Each patient is evaluated in a simulated prospective manner using only the dynamic threshold resulting from the most recent adjustment. Limit thresholds represent the theoretical limit of best dynamic threshold performance by producing the closest possible match between U-Net and PI-RADS performance and are determined from the current cohort. Only fixed and dynamic thresholds can be applied prospectively to new patients, while limit thresholds are an a posteriori reference to judge the success of threshold selection. 

Sensitivity, specificity, and positive and negative predictive value were calculated and compared using the McNemar test [18]. We examined the effect of co-occurrent detection of sPCpositive men, biopsy sextants, and PI-RADS lesions by U-Net and radiologists on the positive (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) using a test based on relative predictive values implemented in the R package DTComPair [19,20]. Statistical analyses were implemented in Python (Python Software Foundation, version 3.7.3, http://www.python.org) and R (R version 3.6.0, R Foundation for Statistical Computing) with details given in Supplementary Material S-4. A p value of 0.05 or less was considered statistically significant. All p values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using Holm's method [21].

documents.snippet: This retrospective bi-national multicenter diagnostic accuracy study evaluated the locked default-threshold performance of a commercial chest radiograph AI system for selected thoracic findings using a CT-anchored, radiographic-detectability reference framework. Consecutive eligible adult patients who underwent frontal chest radiography and chest CT at four tertiary-care centers in Turkey and Bulgaria between June and December 2024 were included. Reference labels were assigned using temporally paired CT, with adjudication of whether CT-confirmed abnormalities had a corresponding radiographic manifestation on the paired chest radiograph. For potentially dynamic findings, the allowable CT–CXR interval was restricted to ≤ 2 days. The AI system was evaluated at the manufacturer’s default threshold of 0.50. Diagnostic performance was summarized using prevalence, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and false-positive burden with 95% confidence intervals. The study included 940 patients with paired CXR-CT examinations. Reference-positive prevalence ranged from 2.2% for pneumothorax to 21.0% for pleural effusion. Sensitivity was highest for fracture (91%) and pneumothorax (90%) and lowest for atelectasis (64%); specificity ranged from 82% for consolidation/opacity to 98% for fracture and pneumothorax. PPV ranged from 43% to 63%, indicating a non-trivial false-positive burden at the evaluated operating point. Because continuous probability scores, human-reader comparison, and workflow outcomes were unavailable, these findings should be interpreted as default-threshold technical validation and support further evaluation of the system as radiologist-supervised decision support with local performance monitoring, rather than standalone diagnosis.

Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were calculated from U-Net probability predictions. U-Net probability thresholds yielding patient-based working points most closely matching PI-RADS ≥ 3 and ≥ 4 performance were obtained as outlined in Supplementary Material S-3. For application to the current cohort, three U-Net thresholds were determined: fixed, dynamic, and limit. Fixed thresholds represent the most straightforward application of the published U-Net to new examinations and are determined from the 300 most recent examinations of the published cohort. Dynamic thresholds are readjusted in regular intervals to keep U-Net and PI-RADS closely matched on the most recent examinations. These are initially set to the values of the fixed thresholds, applied to the 50 following examinations, then repeatedly readjusted using the most recent 300 examinations. Each patient is evaluated in a simulated prospective manner using only the dynamic threshold resulting from the most recent adjustment. Limit thresholds represent the theoretical limit of best dynamic threshold performance by producing the closest possible match between U-Net and PI-RADS performance and are determined from the current cohort. Only fixed and dynamic thresholds can be applied prospectively to new patients, while limit thresholds are an a posteriori reference to judge the success of threshold selection. 

Sensitivity, specificity, and positive and negative predictive value were calculated and compared using the McNemar test [18]. We examined the effect of co-occurrent detection of sPCpositive men, biopsy sextants, and PI-RADS lesions by U-Net and radiologists on the positive (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) using a test based on relative predictive values implemented in the R package DTComPair [19,20]. Statistical analyses were implemented in Python (Python Software Foundation, version 3.7.3, http://www.python.org) and R (R version 3.6.0, R Foundation for Statistical Computing) with details given in Supplementary Material S-4. A p value of 0.05 or less was considered statistically significant. All p values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using Holm's method [21].

Title: Analysis of Pneumonia Area Development in Covid-19 Patients based on Sequential X-Ray Images Using the Seq_UB Architecture
Snippet: In the medical world, segmenting X-ray images is difficult and time-consuming for radiologists. In the case of Covid-19, segmenting the patient's X-ray images can show the specific condition of the Covid-19 patient's lungs. This allows radiologists to diagnose the lung condition of Covid-19 patients quantitatively. In its application, the segmentation process of X-ray images of Covid-19 patients uses a deep learning algorithm. This research develops an image segmentation architecture to obtain a lighter but more accurate image segmentation architecture. The UNet image segmentation architecture is modified by changing the layer arrangement to resemble UBNet [14]. UBNet is a CNN architecture developed explicitly to process chest X-ray images of pneumonia and Covid-19 patients. UBNet is characterized by simple layer arrangement, high accuracy, and low computational load, so the modification of UNet based on the structure of UBNet allows the construction of a lighter and still accurate image segmentation architecture. 

Several image segmentation architectures have been developed, which are shown in Table 5. Some studies, such as FCN, SegNet, and UNet, have shown relatively low evaluation values [23]. Of course, this also depends on the number of datasets used. This study compared the Dice Coefficient values between the standard UNet architecture and Seq_UB with different input image sizes. The results show that reducing the image size does not significantly affect the Dice Coefficient value. This means that reducing the input image size does not significantly affect the accuracy of the segmentation results. However, reducing the input image size will affect the resolution of the segmentation results. Where the smaller the input image size, the lower the resolution obtained. This will have an impact on the final interpretation of the segmentation results. The results show that an input image size of 512 is the best because the resolution of the segmentation results is still very accurate [23]. A recent study in Nature compared various image segmentation models for CXR images. Including input size, total parameters, and DSC values [12]   The results show that reducing the image size does not significantly affect the Dice Coefficient value. This means that reducing the input image size does not significantly affect the accuracy of the segmentation results.

Title: A deep learning segmentation-classification pipeline for X-ray-based COVID-19 diagnosis
Snippet: Typically, patients who end up undergoing a radiological examination end up being patients experiencing increased complications. COVID-GR-1.0 is a small but well-curated dataset that has utility in that it can be employed to determine a classifier's efficacy on weak COVID-19 images. Tabik et al.'s [22] pipeline consisted of a segmentation module and a classification module that performs "inference based on the fusion of CNN twins." [22] The authors used a U-Net [31] segmentation module and trained it on the Montgomery County X-ray dataset [36], the Shenzhen Hospital X-ray datasets [36] and the RSNA Pneumonia CXR challenge dataset [42]. They calculated the smallest rectangle around each segmented image and added a border containing 2.5% of the pixels around each rectangle to obtain their final masked images. The X-rays they segmented were, therefore, never fully masked. The authors did not want to exclude relevant information in these images that could contain useful diagnostic information. After performing binary classification on their segmented COVID-GR-1.0 dataset, Tabik et al.'s [22] classifier obtained a COVID-19 sensitivity of 72.59%. 

Teixeira et al. [23] designed a segmentation-classification pipeline used to diagnose COVID-19 that consisted of a U-Net [31] and Incep-tionV3 [28] CNN. Their U-Net [31] segmentation module was trained on images and masks that were hand-picked from a mixture of public datasets [36,39,43]. The number of images and mask pairings they chose in the Darwin V7 labs [43] segmentation dataset (489) was significantly lower than the total number of pairings available in that dataset (6504). This approach looks as though it allowed them to train their U-Net [31] to have a higher dice similarity coefficient (0.982) than other segmentation units we have seen in the literature for this task. For classification they otherwise used the RYDLS-20 dataset [44].

Title: MultiResUNet for COVID-19 Lung Infection Segmentation Based on CT Image
Snippet: The technical and fundamental requirements of the proposed method will be discussed further in this section. We discuss some related work relevant to the use of Deep Learning on Covid-19 infection segmentation. 

Previous studies have explored lung segmentation on CT images [7], who employed a U-Net architecture for lung cancer detection. Their U-Net-based approach achieved a high segmentation accuracy of 95.02% in DICE metric on a smaller dataset. 

Another study [8] utilized an Encoder and a Decoder Neural Network to segment lung regions in chest X-ray images. They extracted 1736 chest X-ray images from the NIH dataset and performed manual annotations. The segmentation results were evaluated using the MeanIoU metric, achieving 94.9% for two-class segmentation (lung vs. background) and 92% for three-class segmentation (left lung, right lung, vs. background). This paper [9] conducted a comparative study of CNN and U-Net for lung segmentation on 267 CT scan images. The results, evaluated using the DICE metric, demonstrated that U-Net outperformed CNN by a margin of 1.27%, achieving scores of 82.61% and 81.34%, respectively. 

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic underscores the critical need for innovative diagnostic tools. Deep learning-based image segmentation techniques hold significant promise in assisting medical professionals in assessing the pulmonary impact of COVID-19. While visual inspection of CT scans provides valuable information, it may not always be sufficient to comprehensively evaluate the extent and severity of lung infections. Consequently, advanced image processing techniques are essential for a more in-depth analysis. This process typically commences with lung segmentation, followed by further segmentation and classification steps to identify and characterize COVID-19 infections, as previously described in [10]. The authors [11] in "Radiologia serie Radiology and Covid-19" emphasize the superior sensitivity of chest CT scans compared to conventional chest X-rays. CT scans are favored due to their ability to provide a three-dimensional visualization of the lungs. Recent research highlights characteristic CT findings associated with COVID-19 infection.

Title: U-Net Based Chest X-ray Segmentation with Ensemble Classification for Covid-19 and Pneumonia
Snippet: Respiratory diseases have been known to be a main cause of death worldwide. Pneumonia and Covid-19 are two of the dominant diseases. Several deep learning based studies are available in the literature that classifies infection conditions in chest X-ray images. In addition, image segmentation has been also applied to obtain promising results in deep learning approaches. This paper focuses on using a modified version of the U-Net architecture to conduct segmentation on chest X-rays and then use segmented images for classification to assess the impact on the performance. We achieved an Intersection over Union of 93.53% with the proposed modified U-Net architecture and achieved 99.83% accuracy on segmentation aided ensemble classification.

Title: One-Class Classifier for Chest X-ray Anomaly Detection via Contrastive Patch-based Percentile
Snippet: We prepared publicly available data for segmentation and anomaly detection, as listed in Table 1. 

We used public CXR datasets for lung mask segmentation and anomaly detection in various pulmonary diseases. The CXR images and ground-truth lung masks were retrieved from the Japanese Society of Radiological Technology (JSRT) [38] and calculated using segmentation in chest radiographs [40], respectively, from data of 154 nod-   [33] Pneumonia 0 300 COVIDx [33] COVID-19 0 300 [12] Tuberculosis 0 300 ule and 93 non-nodule samples. harder.brainstorming: The seed asks for a default pixel-wise threshold for U-Net models in radiography detection. A retrieval system can easily find papers describing U-Net architectures and their use in medical imaging, and many report threshold values used in their experiments. However, the question presupposes there exists a standard 'default' threshold, when in practice thresholds are highly task-dependent (bone vs soft tissue, segmentation vs detection, different pathologies), imaging modality-dependent (X-ray vs CT), and dataset-dependent. We could force the system to recognize this presupposition is false, or we could require it to reason about WHY no universal default exists by analyzing the dependencies.
harder.chosen_strategy: Require recognition and explanation of task-specific variability that prevents a universal default from existing. The question will ask for the default but contextual factors make this impossible to answer as posed, forcing the system to explain the conditional dependencies rather than retrieve and report a single threshold value.
harder.updated_question: What is the default pixel-wise threshold for U-Net models in radiography detection, and how does it vary across pathology types?
harder.why_harder: The question contains an inherent contradiction: asking for 'the default' while simultaneously asking 'how it varies' exposes that no single default exists. Published U-Net papers in radiography report diverse thresholds (0.3, 0.5, 0.7, etc.) chosen through validation for specific tasks. A retrieval-strong system may simply report the most commonly observed value (e.g., 0.5) as 'the default' without recognizing that threshold selection depends on class imbalance, false positive/negative trade-offs, and pathology characteristics. The system must recognize that thresholds are optimized per-task rather than universally defaulted, and explain the factors (e.g., pneumothorax detection needs high specificity favoring higher thresholds, while lung nodule detection needs high sensitivity favoring lower thresholds) that drive this variability.
harder.verification_criterion: The answer must explicitly state that no universal default pixel-wise threshold exists for U-Net models in radiography detection because optimal thresholds depend on task-specific factors. It must identify at least two concrete pathology-related factors that drive threshold variation with specific directional effects—for example, that pathologies with severe class imbalance require threshold adjustment to balance precision-recall trade-offs, or that life-threatening conditions requiring high sensitivity use lower thresholds while screening applications requiring high specificity use higher thresholds. Fails if it reports a single threshold value (e.g., 0.5) as 'the default' without prominent caveat that this is task-dependent, or if it acknowledges variation but only in generic terms without explaining concrete pathology-related mechanisms that necessitate different thresholds.

Summary
U-Net models for chest radiography commonly produce a pixel-wise probability mask at inference; to obtain a binary lesion/opacity/cavity mask, a per-pixel probability threshold is applied, and performance is typically reported with overlap metrics such as Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and Intersection over Union (IoU). In practice, a 0.5 probability cutoff is a frequent default, but studies show that thresholds are often tuned by pathology due to class imbalance and lesion appearance, with COVID‑19 ground‑glass opacities sometimes requiring lower thresholds and tuberculosis cavities motivating adaptive/intensity‑based strategies in addition to U‑Net lung masking. <cite id="e4906f48-0">In CXR segmentation, U‑Net outputs a sigmoid probability for each pixel (e.g., lung vs background), where values above a threshold define the predicted mask</cite> <cite id="e4906f48-1">A multi‑site multi‑pathology CXR system explicitly set a post‑processing threshold of 0.5 across U‑Net outputs to retain high‑probability regions as pathologies</cite>.

Default pixel‑wise threshold and evaluation practice
- Default convention: many radiography U‑Net pipelines adopt a per‑pixel soft‑threshold of 0.5 to convert the final sigmoid probability layer into a binary mask, aligning with common practice in probabilistic segmentation. <cite id="e4906f48-1">A practical multi‑site study specifies a “Softmax threshold set at 0.5 across all U‑Net outputs” for retaining high‑probability regions as pathologies</cite>. 
- Equivalently, many works evaluate directly on soft outputs via DSC/IoU without explicitly fixing a hard threshold, or on hard masks derived from training/ground truth segmentations; in either case, reported overlaps (Dice ~0.92–0.98) reflect segmentation quality under the chosen thresholding/evaluation scheme. <cite id="24f7434e-0">NIH CXR U‑Net achieved mean Dice 0.9734 and mean IoU 0.9646, evaluated by Dice and IoU over predicted and ground‑truth lung masks</cite> <cite id="24f7434e-1">Across CXR architectures, baseline U‑Net reported Dice 0.9797 and IoU 0.9601; other variants traded boundary errors for slightly higher overlap</cite> <cite id="24f7434e-2">A modified U‑Net on chest radiographs reached Dice up to 0.9040–0.9306 depending on augmentation, again using overlap metrics</cite> <cite id="24f7434e-3">Spine segmentation with U‑Net reported Dice 90.28% and IoU 82.29%, using standard overlap metrics</cite> <cite id="24f7434e-4">A two‑stage CXR U‑Net/ResU‑Net framework reported Dice and accuracy on test sets, indicating high‑quality lung segmentation</cite>. These results imply that with appropriate training and data, per‑pixel thresholding at 0.5 yields clinically useful masks, and evaluation is often summarized via DSC/IoU rather than a single global threshold.

How thresholds vary across pathologies
- COVID‑19 pneumonia on CXR: diffuse ground‑glass opacities and interstitial involvement can be subtle; lowering the per‑pixel threshold increases sensitivity at the cost of noise. <cite id="c56b2ff4-0">One COVID‑19 CXR segmentation study explicitly applied a threshold of 0.2 to the U‑Net’s [0,1] predicted mask, achieving IoU 0.8666 and DSC 0.9273 on validation</cite>. This indicates a pathology‑specific shift from the 0.5 default to a lower cutoff to capture low‑confidence but potentially positive pixels in COVID‑19 opacities.
- Pneumonia and multi‑pathology detection: models trained across normal/COVID/pneumonia often still use 0.5 or similar thresholds, but must contend with class imbalance and overlapping anatomical structures. <cite id="c56b2ff4-3">A CXR dataset and ground‑truth creation pipeline trained a U‑Net on 1500 images (500 normal, 500 COVID‑19, 500 pneumonia), reporting Dice 0.97 and IoU 0.94 on lung segmentation</cite> <cite id="e4906f48-0">CXR datasets are highly unbalanced (lungs occupy much larger area than heart/collarbone), and sigmoid outputs provide per‑pixel probabilities across classes</cite>. In such settings, a one‑size‑fits‑all 0.5 threshold may under‑segment opacities; some pipelines therefore adapt thresholds per class or use ROC‑derived probability cutoffs to balance sensitivity and specificity for opacity detection. <cite id="c56b2ff4-1">A multi‑task COVID‑19 system reported IoU ~0.865–0.885 and high F1 on infected regions, then quantified infected‑pixel percentages relative to lung area to characterize severity</cite>.
- Tuberculosis (TB): workflows often separate lung region first (U‑Net lung mask) and then detect cavities via intensity‑based or adaptive thresholding and shape features, reflecting that cavity boundaries and radiodensity distributions differ from ground‑glass opacities. <cite id="fbd2cfbf-0">A TB detection study used a U‑Net lung mask (Dice 0.9621 on validation) and cropped lung regions for analysis to reduce false positives from heart/spine</cite> <cite id="fbd2cfbf-1">TB cavity identification pipelines compute a pixel‑wise intensity threshold within the lung to segment cavities and extract features for classification</cite> <cite id="fbd2cfbf-2">Other TB cavity methods rely on morphological segmentation and edge enhancement, demonstrating per‑pixel intensity comparisons to cavity thresholds</cite>. For cavity segmentation models, evaluation remains Dice/IoU, but the effective “threshold” spans both the soft U‑Net output (if used) and hard intensity thresholds tailored to lung tissue and cavity contrast. <cite id="fbd2cfbf-3">Tuberculosis cavity segmentation uses Dice and IoU, with larger values indicating better similarity between predicted and true cavity masks</cite>.
- General determinants of threshold choice: lesion appearance (ground‑glass vs nodular/cavitary), background/overlap (heart, spine), and class imbalance drive pathology‑specific thresholds. Multi‑structure CXR images and variability across sites motivate adaptive or multi‑scale thresholding, intensity‑driven priors, and per‑class post‑processing. <cite id="e4906f48-0">U‑Net outputs per‑pixel probabilities across overlapping structures in CXR, necessitating careful thresholding under severe class imbalance</cite> <cite id="e4906f48-1">A multi‑site system explicitly fixes a 0.5 threshold but still reports strong performance, illustrating a pragmatic baseline; site‑specific calibration may be needed</cite> <cite id="fbd2cfbf-1">Adaptive intensity thresholds computed within lung regions are used to separate cavities from normal lung tissue</cite>.

Practical guidance and caveats
- If no pathology‑specific guidance is available, start with a 0.5 per‑pixel threshold on U‑Net’s sigmoid outputs and evaluate via DSC/IoU on test data; then calibrate thresholds per pathology and site using ROC analysis or error‑sensitive review to increase sensitivity for diffuse opacities (e.g., COVID‑19) or tighten specificity for cavity‑like structures (TB). <cite id="e4906f48-1">A 0.5 threshold is a common default across U‑Net outputs in multi‑pathology CXR systems</cite> <cite id="c56b2ff4-0">COVID‑19 CXR segmentation benefits from a lower threshold (0.2) to reach IoU ~0.87 and DSC ~0.93 on validation</cite> <cite id="fbd2cfbf-0">TB pipelines first create a high‑quality lung mask (Dice ~0.96) to constrain analysis, reducing anatomical false positives</cite>.
- Report the exact threshold value and whether evaluation used soft or hard masks, since IoU/DSC can differ substantially with thresholding and intensity normalization choices. <cite id="24f7434e-0">Overlap metrics are standard to report for CXR U‑Net segmentation</cite> <cite id="c56b2ff4-0">Explicit per‑pixel thresholding at 0.2 produced specific IoU/DSC on validation, illustrating sensitivity to threshold selection</cite>.
- In some domains, especially CT‑guided X‑ray projections for COVID‑19, intensity‑based preprocessing and projection algorithms are used before segmentation, further decoupling the “pixel‑wise threshold” concept from pure U‑Net probability cutoffs. <cite id="c56b2ff4-2">A pipeline computes coronal X‑ray projections from CT, then trains Mask R‑CNN for lesion segmentation, achieving IoU ~0.79–0.81; the soft thresholding step is implicit in projection and model outputs</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Default: A per‑pixel probability threshold of 0.5 on the U‑Net’s sigmoid output is a common default baseline for producing binary masks in chest radiography; performance is summarized by Dice/IoU, often around 0.92–0.98 for lung segmentation on standard datasets. <cite id="e4906f48-1">Softmax threshold set at 0.5 across U‑Net outputs</cite> <cite id="24f7434e-0">Mean Dice 0.9734, mean IoU 0.9646 for NIH CXR lung segmentation</cite> <cite id="24f7434e-1">Baseline U‑Net Dice 0.9797, IoU 0.9601 on CXR lung masks</cite>.
- Variation by pathology: COVID‑19 ground‑glass opacities often motivate lowering the per‑pixel threshold (e.g., 0.2) to increase sensitivity, yielding IoU ~0.87 and DSC ~0.93 on validation; pneumonia datasets similarly require handling severe class imbalance and overlapping anatomy. <cite id="c56b2ff4-0">COVID‑19 CXR: threshold 0.2 → IoU 0.8666, DSC 0.9273</cite> <cite id="e4906f48-0">CXR class imbalance and overlapping structures necessitate careful thresholding</cite> <cite id="c56b2ff4-3">U‑Net lung segmentation across normal/COVID/pneumonia achieved Dice 0.97 and IoU 0.94</cite>.
- TB: U‑Net lung masking with Dice ~0.96 is used to crop the region of interest; cavity detection frequently combines U‑Net with adaptive intensity‑based thresholds and feature‑driven classification, with Dice/IoU used to quantify cavity segmentation quality. <cite id="fbd2cfbf-0">U‑Net lung mask Dice 0.9621; cropping lung ROI reduces extraneous structures</cite> <cite id="fbd2cfbf-1">Adaptive pixel‑intensity thresholds within lung regions to segment cavities</cite> <cite id="fbd2cfbf-3">Dice and IoU remain the primary evaluation metrics for cavity segmentation</cite>.

Snippet: We propose a fully automated pipeline to segment COVID-19 lung opacities on chest X-rays. A limitation of our study is that we used small amounts of publicly available data; however, our results still suggest that improved accuracy can be obtained by augmenting chest X-ray data with large numbers of frontal projections of public CT volumes. Title: Novel coarse-to-fine dual scale technique for tuberculosis cavity detection in chest radiographs
Snippet: Although many lung disease diagnostic procedures can benefit from computer-aided detection (CAD), current CAD systems are mainly designed for lung nodule detection. In this article, we focus on tuberculosis (TB) cavity detection because of its highly infectious nature. Infectious TB, such as adult-type pulmonary TB (APTB) and HIV-related TB, continues to be a public health problem of global proportion, especially in the developing countries. Cavities in the upper lung zone provide a useful cue to radiologists for potential infectious TB. However, the superimposed anatomical structures in the lung field hinder effective identification of these cavities. In order to address the deficiency of existing computer-aided TB cavity detection methods, we propose an efficient coarse-to-fine dual scale technique for cavity detection in chest radiographs. Gaussian-based matching, local binary pattern, and gradient orientation features are applied at the coarse scale, while circularity, gradient inverse coefficient of variation and Kullback–Leibler divergence measures are applied at the fine scale. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed technique outperforms other existing techniques with respect to true cavity detection rate and segmentation accuracy.

Snippet: The U-Net model is widely used due to its efficiency and effectiveness in solving various image segmentation problems, especially in the field of medical imaging (Ronneberger et al., 2015). The U-Net architecture is characterized by a symmetrical "U-shaped" design, which consists of two main parts: compression (encoder) and expansion (decoder). 

In the context of chest X-ray segmentation, U-Net is particularly well suited for several reasons: 

• The model's ability to work at different scales makes it effective in recognizing the fine details needed to accurately delineate anatomical structures such as lungs, heart, and collarbones. • Medical images can vary greatly in terms of structure visibility due to different patient positions, pathologies, or imaging conditions. U-Net's robust learning and generalization capabilities make it effective in handling this variability. 

• For this work, the integration of edge enhancement techniques before image input into the U-Net model can further improve its ability to accurately detect and segment relevant medical structures. By using edge detection to enhance the boundaries, the U-Net model is able to capture fine details and improve segmentation accuracy. 

The model uses a sigmoid activation function on the output layer. In this case, classes can overlap (i.e., one-pixel region can simultaneously belong to several classes), so using a sigmoid activation function for each channel of the output layer may be a better option than the softmax function. 

The formula of the sigmoid function (Xu et al., 2021;Kovtun et al., 2023): 

where x is the input signal to the neuron. The sigmoid activation function processes each output channel independently. Each channel of the output layer represents the probability that a pixel belongs to a certain class. For example, if the output layer has three channels for three different classes (lungs, heart, collarbone), each channel gives the probability of belonging to each of these classes. 

In the semantic segmentation problem, when there are classes such as lungs, heart, and collarbones in medical images, the dataset is considered unbalanced. Despite the fact that each image contains all three classes, the lungs in X-ray images occupy a much larger area compared to the heart and collarbones.

Title: MDU-Net: A Convolutional Network for Clavicle and Rib Segmentation from a Chest Radiograph
Snippet: Automatic bone segmentation from a chest radiograph is an important and challenging task in medical image analysis. However, a chest radiograph contains numerous artifacts and tissue shadows, such as trachea, blood vessels, and lung veins, which limit the accuracy of traditional segmentation methods, such as thresholding and contour-related techniques. Deep learning has recently achieved excellent segmentation of some organs, such as the pancreas and the hippocampus. However, the insufficiency of annotated datasets impedes clavicle and rib segmentation from chest X-rays. We have constructed a dataset of chest X-rays with a raw chest radiograph and four annotated images showing the clavicles, anterior ribs, posterior ribs, and all bones (the complete set of ribs and clavicle). On the basis of a sufficient dataset, a multitask dense connection U-Net (MDU-Net) is proposed to address the challenge of bone segmentation from a chest radiograph. We first combine the U-Net multiscale feature fusion method, DenseNet dense connection, and multitasking mechanism to construct the proposed network referred to as MDU-Net. We then present a mask encoding mechanism that can force the network to learn the background features. Transfer learning is ultimately introduced to help the network extract sufficient features. We evaluate the proposed network by fourfold cross validation on 88 chest radiography images. The proposed method achieves the average DSC (Dice similarity coefficient) values of 93.78%, 80.95%, 89.06%, and 88.38% in clavicle segmentation, anterior rib segmentation, posterior rib segmentation, and segmentation of all bones, respectively.
