Summary
U-Net models for chest radiography commonly produce a pixel-wise probability mask at inference; to obtain a binary lesion/opacity/cavity mask, a per-pixel probability threshold is applied, and performance is typically reported with overlap metrics such as Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and Intersection over Union (IoU). In practice, a 0.5 probability cutoff is a frequent default, but studies show that thresholds are often tuned by pathology due to class imbalance and lesion appearance, with COVID‑19 ground‑glass opacities sometimes requiring lower thresholds and tuberculosis cavities motivating adaptive/intensity‑based strategies in addition to U‑Net lung masking. <cite id="e4906f48-0">In CXR segmentation, U‑Net outputs a sigmoid probability for each pixel (e.g., lung vs background), where values above a threshold define the predicted mask</cite> <cite id="e4906f48-1">A multi‑site multi‑pathology CXR system explicitly set a post‑processing threshold of 0.5 across U‑Net outputs to retain high‑probability regions as pathologies</cite>.

Default pixel‑wise threshold and evaluation practice
- Default convention: many radiography U‑Net pipelines adopt a per‑pixel soft‑threshold of 0.5 to convert the final sigmoid probability layer into a binary mask, aligning with common practice in probabilistic segmentation. <cite id="e4906f48-1">A practical multi‑site study specifies a “Softmax threshold set at 0.5 across all U‑Net outputs” for retaining high‑probability regions as pathologies</cite>. 
- Equivalently, many works evaluate directly on soft outputs via DSC/IoU without explicitly fixing a hard threshold, or on hard masks derived from training/ground truth segmentations; in either case, reported overlaps (Dice ~0.92–0.98) reflect segmentation quality under the chosen thresholding/evaluation scheme. <cite id="24f7434e-0">NIH CXR U‑Net achieved mean Dice 0.9734 and mean IoU 0.9646, evaluated by Dice and IoU over predicted and ground‑truth lung masks</cite> <cite id="24f7434e-1">Across CXR architectures, baseline U‑Net reported Dice 0.9797 and IoU 0.9601; other variants traded boundary errors for slightly higher overlap</cite> <cite id="24f7434e-2">A modified U‑Net on chest radiographs reached Dice up to 0.9040–0.9306 depending on augmentation, again using overlap metrics</cite> <cite id="24f7434e-3">Spine segmentation with U‑Net reported Dice 90.28% and IoU 82.29%, using standard overlap metrics</cite> <cite id="24f7434e-4">A two‑stage CXR U‑Net/ResU‑Net framework reported Dice and accuracy on test sets, indicating high‑quality lung segmentation</cite>. These results imply that with appropriate training and data, per‑pixel thresholding at 0.5 yields clinically useful masks, and evaluation is often summarized via DSC/IoU rather than a single global threshold.

How thresholds vary across pathologies
- COVID‑19 pneumonia on CXR: diffuse ground‑glass opacities and interstitial involvement can be subtle; lowering the per‑pixel threshold increases sensitivity at the cost of noise. <cite id="c56b2ff4-0">One COVID‑19 CXR segmentation study explicitly applied a threshold of 0.2 to the U‑Net’s [0,1] predicted mask, achieving IoU 0.8666 and DSC 0.9273 on validation</cite>. This indicates a pathology‑specific shift from the 0.5 default to a lower cutoff to capture low‑confidence but potentially positive pixels in COVID‑19 opacities.
- Pneumonia and multi‑pathology detection: models trained across normal/COVID/pneumonia often still use 0.5 or similar thresholds, but must contend with class imbalance and overlapping anatomical structures. <cite id="c56b2ff4-3">A CXR dataset and ground‑truth creation pipeline trained a U‑Net on 1500 images (500 normal, 500 COVID‑19, 500 pneumonia), reporting Dice 0.97 and IoU 0.94 on lung segmentation</cite> <cite id="e4906f48-0">CXR datasets are highly unbalanced (lungs occupy much larger area than heart/collarbone), and sigmoid outputs provide per‑pixel probabilities across classes</cite>. In such settings, a one‑size‑fits‑all 0.5 threshold may under‑segment opacities; some pipelines therefore adapt thresholds per class or use ROC‑derived probability cutoffs to balance sensitivity and specificity for opacity detection. <cite id="c56b2ff4-1">A multi‑task COVID‑19 system reported IoU ~0.865–0.885 and high F1 on infected regions, then quantified infected‑pixel percentages relative to lung area to characterize severity</cite>.
- Tuberculosis (TB): workflows often separate lung region first (U‑Net lung mask) and then detect cavities via intensity‑based or adaptive thresholding and shape features, reflecting that cavity boundaries and radiodensity distributions differ from ground‑glass opacities. <cite id="fbd2cfbf-0">A TB detection study used a U‑Net lung mask (Dice 0.9621 on validation) and cropped lung regions for analysis to reduce false positives from heart/spine</cite> <cite id="fbd2cfbf-1">TB cavity identification pipelines compute a pixel‑wise intensity threshold within the lung to segment cavities and extract features for classification</cite> <cite id="fbd2cfbf-2">Other TB cavity methods rely on morphological segmentation and edge enhancement, demonstrating per‑pixel intensity comparisons to cavity thresholds</cite>. For cavity segmentation models, evaluation remains Dice/IoU, but the effective “threshold” spans both the soft U‑Net output (if used) and hard intensity thresholds tailored to lung tissue and cavity contrast. <cite id="fbd2cfbf-3">Tuberculosis cavity segmentation uses Dice and IoU, with larger values indicating better similarity between predicted and true cavity masks</cite>.
- General determinants of threshold choice: lesion appearance (ground‑glass vs nodular/cavitary), background/overlap (heart, spine), and class imbalance drive pathology‑specific thresholds. Multi‑structure CXR images and variability across sites motivate adaptive or multi‑scale thresholding, intensity‑driven priors, and per‑class post‑processing. <cite id="e4906f48-0">U‑Net outputs per‑pixel probabilities across overlapping structures in CXR, necessitating careful thresholding under severe class imbalance</cite> <cite id="e4906f48-1">A multi‑site system explicitly fixes a 0.5 threshold but still reports strong performance, illustrating a pragmatic baseline; site‑specific calibration may be needed</cite> <cite id="fbd2cfbf-1">Adaptive intensity thresholds computed within lung regions are used to separate cavities from normal lung tissue</cite>.

Practical guidance and caveats
- If no pathology‑specific guidance is available, start with a 0.5 per‑pixel threshold on U‑Net’s sigmoid outputs and evaluate via DSC/IoU on test data; then calibrate thresholds per pathology and site using ROC analysis or error‑sensitive review to increase sensitivity for diffuse opacities (e.g., COVID‑19) or tighten specificity for cavity‑like structures (TB). <cite id="e4906f48-1">A 0.5 threshold is a common default across U‑Net outputs in multi‑pathology CXR systems</cite> <cite id="c56b2ff4-0">COVID‑19 CXR segmentation benefits from a lower threshold (0.2) to reach IoU ~0.87 and DSC ~0.93 on validation</cite> <cite id="fbd2cfbf-0">TB pipelines first create a high‑quality lung mask (Dice ~0.96) to constrain analysis, reducing anatomical false positives</cite>.

Title: Comparative evaluation of deep learning models for lung segmentation in chest X-rays: applications in infectious disease screening
Snippet: This section presents the experimental results. The comparative evaluation of ten deep learning architectures for lung segmentation from chest X-rays provides valuable insights into their relative strengths and limitations. Performance was assessed using Dice Coefficient, Intersection over Union (IoU), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Hausdorff Distance, and Average Symmetric Surface Distance (ASSD), which together capture both overlap accuracy and boundary precision. As shown in Table 1 and Fig. 5, the quantitative performance of CNN-based segmentation models on chest X-ray images demonstrates that the Attention-UNet outperforms the standard UNet across all evaluation metrics, including Dice Coefficient, IoU, Mean Absolute Error, and Hausdorff Distance. 

The baseline U-Net achieved strong results, with a Dice score of 0.9797 and an IoU of 0.9601, confirming its reliability as a foundational model. However, its higher MAE (3.01) and Hausdorff Distance (16.85) suggest boundary inconsistencies. This can be attributed to error propagation across the cascaded U-Net stages, which refine predictions but may amplify small inaccuracies.The U2-Net stood out for achieving the lowest MAE (1.70) and a relatively low Hausdorff Distance (13.57), demonstrating precise pixel-level predictions and good boundary adherence. This section presents the experimental results. The comparative evaluation of ten deep learning architectures for lung segmentation from chest X-rays provides valuable insights into their relative strengths and limitations. Performance was assessed using Dice Coefficient, Intersection over Union (IoU), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Hausdorff Distance, and Average Symmetric Surface Distance (ASSD), which together capture both overlap accuracy and boundary precision. As shown in Table 1 and Fig. 5, the quantitative performance of CNN-based segmentation models on chest X-ray images demonstrates that the Attention-UNet outperforms the standard UNet across all evaluation metrics, including Dice Coefficient, IoU, Mean Absolute Error, and Hausdorff Distance. 

The baseline U-Net achieved strong results, with a Dice score of 0.9797 and an IoU of 0.9601, confirming its reliability as a foundational model. However, its Hausdorff Distance of 15.66 indicates moderate boundary localization errors, suggesting that while U-Net performs well in general lung delineation, it struggles with finer boundary details.The Attention U-Net improved slightly on overlap metrics (Dice: 0.9816, IoU: 0.9638) but introduced a higher MAE (2.76) and Hausdorff Distance (16.27). This implies that while the attention mechanism enhances focus on salient lung regions, it may overfit certain structures, leading to less consistent pixel-level accuracy.The Double U-Net delivered one of the highest Dice scores (0.9843) and IoU (0.9691), reflecting excellent segmentation overlap. However, its higher MAE (3.01) and Hausdorff Distance (16.85) suggest boundary inconsistencies. This can be attributed to error propagation across the cascaded U-Net stages, which refine predictions but may amplify small inaccuracies.The U2-Net stood out for achieving the lowest MAE (1.70) and a relatively low Hausdorff Distance (13.57), demonstrating precise pixel-level predictions and good boundary adherence. snippet.text: The purpose of this research is to segment the chest on X-rays, a crucial step in medical image processing pivotal for diagnosing and treating lung diseases. By employing modifications to the U-Net model, this study endeavors to enhance chest segmentation on X-rays. The approach includes introducing alterations to the basic architecture of the U-Net model, integrating Inception blocks, and a using a squeeze-and-excitation mechanism to improve segmentation accuracy. The Shenzhen dataset, comprising chest radiographs, serves as the subject of investigation, highlighting the practical application of these modifications. The utilization of the MIU-Net model for automatic chest organ segmentation underscores its significance in the realm of lung disease diagnosis and treatment. Experimental methodologies encompass two types of data augmentation: Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) and the introduction of Gaussian noise, to test the model's robustness under various conditions. A comparative analysis is conducted against both the baseline U-Net and U-Net with Inception blocks. The results show that the improved U-Net model that includes Inception and Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) is a lot better than the original U-Net. Specifically, the Dice coefficient for the improved model stands at 0.9040 for the original data, 0.9306 with CLAHE application, and 0.9232 with Gaussian noise addition. These findings underscore the importance of the research, emphasizing the significance of improving the accuracy of chest segmentation on X-rays for early disease detection and treatment optimization, which are the practical implications of this study. The research’s implications extend beyond academic interest, offering potential enhancements in clinical practices for lung disease management.

Title: COVID_MTNet: COVID-19 Detection with Multi-Task Deep Learning Approaches
Snippet: For further evaluation and to define the specific infected regions with COVID-19, we have implemented an end to end segmentation system for extracting the chest regions from the entire X-ray images. 

The NABLA-N network was used for chest segmentation from X-ray images. This model was trained on the chest-xray segmentation challenge dataset. After successfully training the model, the performance was evaluated on the testing samples provided by the organizer. We have tested on completely new 57 chest X-ray images. The model shows 0.9452 and 0.9466 in terms of global accuracy and F1-score respectively. In addition, it shows around 0.8650 and 0.8846 for Intersection over Union (IoU) and Dice similarity Coefficient score (DC). 

The experimental results for the segmentation model for COVID-19 X-ray samples are shown in Figure 12. The first column shows the inputs images, the second column shows the outputs from COVID-Seg_X-ray, the third column shows the polished segmentation masks, the fourth column represents outputs for only chest regions, and the fifth column shows the final outputs with COVID-19 infected regions. The qualitative results clearly demonstrate that the proposed model is able to segment and detect contaminated regions of COVID-19 accurately from the chest X-ray images. 

In addition, for quantitative justification, we have calculated the total number of pixels of the lung regions and the total number of pixels for infected regions with COVID-19. The percentage is calculated with respect to the total areas of the lung, which can be used for measuring the contingency and severity of corona-virus patients. For the first row and third column in Figure 12, the number of total pixels for lung is 6,696 and total number of infected pixels with COVID-19 is 2,245. Thus, the percentage of infection is 33.52% with respect to the total number of pixels of lung regions. In the last row of Figure 12, the total number of pixels for the lung regions is 9,601 and the total number of infected pixels with COVID-19 is 3,609. Thus the percentage of infection is 37.58%. 

This quantitative analysis can be applied to define the severity of the COVID-19 disease.

Title: COVID-19 Lung Lesion Segmentation Using a Sparsely Supervised Mask R-CNN on Chest X-rays Automatically Computed from Volumetric CTs
Snippet: We propose a fully automated pipeline to segment COVID-19 lung opacities on chest X-rays. The majority of current work regarding COVID-19 opacity segmentation has been in CT imaging; however, since chest X-rays are much more commonly obtained than CTs, COVID-19 lung disease segmentation on chest X-ray images could enable the development of artificial intelligence applications that use these images to assess disease severity and evaluate or predict progression. Our model first utilizes a pixel-based summation algorithm to compute a coronal X-ray projection from axial CT and mask volumes. A floodfill-and hull-based approach is then employed to generate labels for each chest X-ray projection, which are used to train a Mask R-CNN for the task of instance segmentation. Our model achieved an IOU score of 0.81 ± 0.03 when trained on Dataset 1, and an IOU score of 0.79 ± 0.03 when trained on Dataset 2. A small number of chest X-rays compared to the number of frontal projections was chosen for Dataset 2 in order to demonstrate the potential for X-ray projections from CT volumes to replace actual chest X-rays as training samples for deep learning models. 

A limitation of our study is that we used small amounts of publicly available data; however, our results still suggest that improved accuracy can be obtained by augmenting chest X-ray data with large numbers of frontal projections of public CT volumes. Training and testing our model on larger datasets could improve future results.

Title: Chest X-ray dataset and ground truth for lung segmentation
Snippet: Fig. 2 shows the data curation process. U-Net model was trained using chest X-ray datasets derived from other repository sources, namely datasets from Qatar University, which already have ground truth with a total of 1500 data of 500 covid-19, pneumonia, and normal images in each class. The accuracy level produced by this model is DSC (Dice Similarity Coefficient) of 97 % and IoU (Intersection over Union) of 94 %. This model will later be used to segment the chest X-ray image from Universitas Airlangga Hospital because the dataset provided by the hospital still needs to have ground truth. 

The chest X-ray image dataset from Universitas Airlangga Hospital amounted to 657 images in DICOM format, which were then converted into .bmp format using Python programming. The images that were successfully converted into .bmp format amounted to 371 images consisting of 273 images infected with covid-19, 59 images infected with pneumonia, and 39 normal images. 

Images that have been converted into .bmp format are then predicted using the U-Net model that has been created to produce segmented images. Furthermore, line annotation is made following image segmentation results and overlaps on the chest X-ray image according to the radiologist's request to be shown to the radiologist and validated. 

From the 371 images submitted to radiologists, there were 292 segmented images validated to be accurate by radiologists, consisting of 207 images infected with Covid-19, 53 images infected with pneumonia, and 32 images normal. These validated images are then collected and stored in a dataset repository. Fig. 3 shows an example of a merged chest X-ray image, line annotation, and radiologically validated segmentation results.

Title: MultiResUNet for COVID-19 Lung Infection Segmentation Based on CT Image
Snippet: The technical and fundamental requirements of the proposed method will be discussed further in this section. We discuss some related work relevant to the use of Deep Learning on Covid-19 infection segmentation. 

Previous studies have explored lung segmentation on CT images [7], who employed a U-Net architecture for lung cancer detection. Their U-Net-based approach achieved a high segmentation accuracy of 95.02% in DICE metric on a smaller dataset. 

Another study [8] utilized an Encoder and a Decoder Neural Network to segment lung regions in chest X-ray images. They extracted 1736 chest X-ray images from the NIH dataset and performed manual annotations. The segmentation results were evaluated using the MeanIoU metric, achieving 94.9% for two-class segmentation (lung vs. background) and 92% for three-class segmentation (left lung, right lung, vs. background). This paper [9] conducted a comparative study of CNN and U-Net for lung segmentation on 267 CT scan images. The results, evaluated using the DICE metric, demonstrated that U-Net outperformed CNN by a margin of 1.27%, achieving scores of 82.61% and 81.34%, respectively. 

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic underscores the critical need for innovative diagnostic tools. Deep learning-based image segmentation techniques hold significant promise in assisting medical professionals in assessing the pulmonary impact of COVID-19. While visual inspection of CT scans provides valuable information, it may not always be sufficient to comprehensively evaluate the extent and severity of lung infections. Consequently, advanced image processing techniques are essential for a more in-depth analysis. This process typically commences with lung segmentation, followed by further segmentation and classification steps to identify and characterize COVID-19 infections, as previously described in [10]. The authors [11] in "Radiologia serie Radiology and Covid-19" emphasize the superior sensitivity of chest CT scans compared to conventional chest X-rays. CT scans are favored due to their ability to provide a three-dimensional visualization of the lungs. Recent research highlights characteristic CT findings associated with COVID-19 infection.

Previous studies have explored lung segmentation on CT images [7], who employed a U-Net architecture for lung cancer detection. Their U-Net-based approach achieved a high segmentation accuracy of 95.02% in DICE metric on a smaller dataset. 

Another study [8] utilized an Encoder and a Decoder Neural Network to segment lung regions in chest X-ray images. They extracted 1736 chest X-ray images from the NIH dataset and performed manual annotations. The segmentation results were evaluated using the MeanIoU metric, achieving 94.9% for two-class segmentation (lung vs. background) and 92% for three-class segmentation (left lung, right lung, vs. background). This paper [9] conducted a comparative study of CNN and U-Net for lung segmentation on 267 CT scan images. The results, evaluated using the DICE metric, demonstrated that U-Net outperformed CNN by a margin of 1.27%, achieving scores of 82.61% and 81.34%, respectively. 

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic underscores the critical need for innovative diagnostic tools. Deep learning-based image segmentation techniques hold significant promise in assisting medical professionals in assessing the pulmonary impact of COVID-19. While visual inspection of CT scans provides valuable information, it may not always be sufficient to comprehensively evaluate the extent and severity of lung infections. Consequently, advanced image processing techniques are essential for a more in-depth analysis. This process typically commences with lung segmentation, followed by further segmentation and classification steps to identify and characterize COVID-19 infections, as previously described in [10]. documents.title: COVID-19 Lung Lesion Segmentation Using a Sparsely Supervised Mask R-CNN on Chest X-rays Automatically Computed from Volumetric CTs
documents.snippet:
We propose a fully automated pipeline to segment COVID-19 lung opacities on chest X-rays. The majority of current work regarding COVID-19 opacity segmentation has been in CT imaging; however, since chest X-rays are much more commonly obtained than CTs, COVID-19 lung disease segmentation on chest X-ray images could enable the development of artificial intelligence applications that use these images to assess disease severity and evaluate or predict progression. Our model first utilizes a pixel-based summation algorithm to compute a coronal X-ray projection from axial CT and mask volumes. A floodfill-and hull-based approach is then employed to generate labels for each chest X-ray projection, which are used to train a Mask R-CNN for the task of instance segmentation. Our model achieved an IOU score of 0.81 ± 0.03 when trained on Dataset 1, and an IOU score of 0.79 ± 0.03 when trained on Dataset 2. A small number of chest X-rays compared to the number of frontal projections was chosen for Dataset 2 in order to demonstrate the potential for X-ray projections from CT volumes to replace actual chest X-rays as training samples for deep learning models. 

A limitation of our study is that we used small amounts of publicly available data; however, our results still suggest that improved accuracy can be obtained by augmenting chest X-ray data with large numbers of frontal projections of public CT volumes. Training and testing our model on larger datasets could improve future results.

Title: Deep Learning Algorithms with Demographic Information Help to Detect Tuberculosis in Chest Radiographs in Annual Workers’ Health Examination Data
Snippet: Chest X-rays often include structures other than lungs, such as the spine and heart. As these areas are not useful for, and may hinder, the prediction of tuberculosis, we generated a mask containing lung structures only using U-Net [14]-a deep learning algorithm for biomedical image segmentation. Title: An Adaptive Region Growing Algorithm with Support Vector Machine Classifier for Tuberculosis Cavity Identification
Snippet: The process of this work is precisely explained in the Fig. 1 as block diagram. In this figure, some sample chest x-ray images with tuberculosis and without tuberculosis. The sample images are then preprocessed and then send for segmenting the lung and cavity regions. After the lung and cavity regions are segmented from the sample images, some parameters are chosen to train the classifier. Title: Novel coarse-to-fine dual scale technique for tuberculosis cavity detection in chest radiographs
Snippet: Although many lung disease diagnostic procedures can benefit from computer-aided detection (CAD), current CAD systems are mainly designed for lung nodule detection. In this article, we focus on tuberculosis (TB) cavity detection because of its highly infectious nature. Infectious TB, such as adult-type pulmonary TB (APTB) and HIV-related TB, continues to be a public health problem of global proportion, especially in the developing countries. Cavities in the upper lung zone provide a useful cue to radiologists for potential infectious TB. However, the superimposed anatomical structures in the lung field hinder effective identification of these cavities. In order to address the deficiency of existing computer-aided TB cavity detection methods, we propose an efficient coarse-to-fine dual scale technique for cavity detection in chest radiographs. Gaussian-based matching, local binary pattern, and gradient orientation features are applied at the coarse scale, while circularity, gradient inverse coefficient of variation and Kullback–Leibler divergence measures are applied at the fine scale. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed technique outperforms other existing techniques with respect to true cavity detection rate and segmentation accuracy.

Title: Approach for enhancing the accuracy of semantic segmentation of chest X-ray images by edge detection and deep learning integration
Snippet: The U-Net model is widely used due to its efficiency and effectiveness in solving various image segmentation problems, especially in the field of medical imaging (Ronneberger et al., 2015). The U-Net architecture is characterized by a symmetrical "U-shaped" design, which consists of two main parts: compression (encoder) and expansion (decoder). 

In the context of chest X-ray segmentation, U-Net is particularly well suited for several reasons: 

• The model's ability to work at different scales makes it effective in recognizing the fine details needed to accurately delineate anatomical structures such as lungs, heart, and collarbones. • Medical images can vary greatly in terms of structure visibility due to different patient positions, pathologies, or imaging conditions. U-Net's robust learning and generalization capabilities make it effective in handling this variability. 

• For this work, the integration of edge enhancement techniques before image input into the U-Net model can further improve its ability to accurately detect and segment relevant medical structures. By using edge detection to enhance the boundaries, the U-Net model is able to capture fine details and improve segmentation accuracy. 

The model uses a sigmoid activation function on the output layer. In this case, classes can overlap (i.e., one-pixel region can simultaneously belong to several classes), so using a sigmoid activation function for each channel of the output layer may be a better option than the softmax function. 

The formula of the sigmoid function (Xu et al., 2021;Kovtun et al., 2023): 

where x is the input signal to the neuron. The sigmoid activation function processes each output channel independently. Each channel of the output layer represents the probability that a pixel belongs to a certain class. For example, if the output layer has three channels for three different classes (lungs, heart, collarbone), each channel gives the probability of belonging to each of these classes. 

In the semantic segmentation problem, when there are classes such as lungs, heart, and collarbones in medical images, the dataset is considered unbalanced. Despite the fact that each image contains all three classes, the lungs in X-ray images occupy a much larger area compared to the heart and collarbones.

Title: NextGen lung disease diagnosis with explainable artificial intelligence
Snippet: Lung anomalies reveal details about a wide range of illnesses which has more overlapping radiological features, such as ground glass opacities (GGO), paving patterns, reverse halo signs etc. To ascertain what type of lung condition the patient is affected with, our study looks at the CXR with a radical approach. An extra lung segmentation component is added to the pipeline to improve the performance of the proposed model's detection and explanation components. Manual segmentation is not feasible for CXR images since it has air bronchograms and cavitary lesions. Furthermore, errors and contradictions can arise from human annotations. Thus, the proposed Lung segmentation forces the segmentation of multiclass images and its explanation networks to only detect and explain in the lung sector of the images by feeding them veiled lung images. The explanation section's output is displayed in the entire CXR for a more accurate understanding. 

The U-Net model is a well-known deep-learning architecture designed for image segmentation tasks, such as lung segmentation. The proposed model is shown in Fig. 2. Using chest X-rays with dimensions of 256 × 256 × 3  as input images produces binary segmentation masks representing the lungs. The U-Net model was trained on a publicly available dataset containing chest X-ray images and their corresponding masks 41,42 . The U-Net model uses encoder and decoder structures to process the input images and generate a binary mask representing the lungs. The encoder captures high-level abstractions through convolutional and pooling layers, gradually reducing the spatial dimension and increasing the number of filters to extract hierarchical features. On the other hand, the decoder pathway utilizes skip connections that concatenate feature maps from corresponding layers in the encoder, allowing the recovery of the original image resolution while retaining crucial contextual information. Deconvolution layers (transposed convolutions) have been included to enhance the feature maps. 

The model outputs a single pixel-wise probability map with a sigmoid activation function. The final output is a binary segmentation mask of the lungs. This improved U-Net effectively analyze X-ray images of the lung by segmenting and interpreting all parts, including the infected and uninfected regions in the lung.

Title: MDU-Net: A Convolutional Network for Clavicle and Rib Segmentation from a Chest Radiograph
Snippet: Automatic bone segmentation from a chest radiograph is an important and challenging task in medical image analysis. However, a chest radiograph contains numerous artifacts and tissue shadows, such as trachea, blood vessels, and lung veins, which limit the accuracy of traditional segmentation methods, such as thresholding and contour-related techniques. Deep learning has recently achieved excellent segmentation of some organs, such as the pancreas and the hippocampus. snippet.text:
The U-Net model is widely used due to its efficiency and effectiveness in solving various image segmentation problems, especially in the field of medical imaging (Ronneberger et al., 2015). The U-Net architecture is characterized by a symmetrical "U-shaped" design, which consists of two main parts: compression (encoder) and expansion (decoder). 

In the context of chest X-ray segmentation, U-Net is particularly well suited for several reasons: 

• The model's ability to work at different scales makes it effective in recognizing the fine details needed to accurately delineate anatomical structures such as lungs, heart, and collarbones. • Medical images can vary greatly in terms of structure visibility due to different patient positions, pathologies, or imaging conditions. U-Net's robust learning and generalization capabilities make it effective in handling this variability. 

• For this work, the integration of edge enhancement techniques before image input into the U-Net model can further improve its ability to accurately detect and segment relevant medical structures. By using edge detection to enhance the boundaries, the U-Net model is able to capture fine details and improve segmentation accuracy. 

The model uses a sigmoid activation function on the output layer. In this case, classes can overlap (i.e., one-pixel region can simultaneously belong to several classes), so using a sigmoid activation function for each channel of the output layer may be a better option than the softmax function. 

The formula of the sigmoid function (Xu et al., 2021;Kovtun et al., 2023): 

where x is the input signal to the neuron. The sigmoid activation function processes each output channel independently. Each channel of the output layer represents the probability that a pixel belongs to a certain class. For example, if the output layer has three channels for three different classes (lungs, heart, collarbone), each channel gives the probability of belonging to each of these classes. 

In the semantic segmentation problem, when there are classes such as lungs, heart, and collarbones in medical images, the dataset is considered unbalanced. Despite the fact that each image contains all three classes, the lungs in X-ray images occupy a much larger area compared to the heart and collarbones.

snippet.text:
Lung anomalies reveal details about a wide range of illnesses which has more overlapping radiological features, such as ground glass opacities (GGO), paving patterns, reverse halo signs etc. To ascertain what type of lung condition the patient is affected with, our study looks at the CXR with a radical approach. An extra lung segmentation component is added to the pipeline to improve the performance of the proposed model's detection and explanation components. Manual segmentation is not feasible for CXR images since it has air bronchograms and cavitary lesions. Furthermore, errors and contradictions can arise from human annotations. Thus, the proposed Lung segmentation forces the segmentation of multiclass images and its explanation networks to only detect and explain in the lung sector of the images by feeding them veiled lung images. The explanation section's output is displayed in the entire CXR for a more accurate understanding. 

The U-Net model is a well-known deep-learning architecture designed for image segmentation tasks, such as lung segmentation. The proposed model is shown in Fig. 2. Using chest X-rays with dimensions of 256 × 256 × 3  as input images produces binary segmentation masks representing the lungs. The U-Net model was trained on a publicly available dataset containing chest X-ray images and their corresponding masks 41,42 . The U-Net model uses encoder and decoder structures to process the input images and generate a binary mask representing the lungs. The encoder captures high-level abstractions through convolutional and pooling layers, gradually reducing the spatial dimension and increasing the number of filters to extract hierarchical features. On the other hand, the decoder pathway utilizes skip connections that concatenate feature maps from corresponding layers in the encoder, allowing the recovery of the original image resolution while retaining crucial contextual information. Deconvolution layers (transposed convolutions) have been included to enhance the feature maps. 

The model outputs a single pixel-wise probability map with a sigmoid activation function. The final output is a binary segmentation mask of the lungs. This improved U-Net effectively analyze X-ray images of the lung by segmenting and interpreting all parts, including the infected and uninfected regions in the lung.

attempts.answer:
Summary recommendation
- Start with a per‑pixel probability threshold of 0.5 on the U‑Net’s softmax output, binarize the mask (pixels > 0.5 become 1), then apply morphology (e.g., closing to connect small breaks), followed by connected‑component analysis, keep only the largest component per anatomical region (e.g., per lung/mediastinum), and fill holes; this combination is widely used for radiographic lesion detection and yields a practical, tunable pipeline. <cite id="ba08c7ce-1">A U‑Net‑based chest X‑ray system retained high‑probability regions using a softmax threshold of 0.5</cite> <cite id="ba08c7ce-3">A lesion‑likelihood map can be thresholded (e.g., Otsu) to get a binary mask, then reduced to the largest connected component and finalized by whole‑filling</cite> <cite id="ba08c7ce-4">For pulmonary nodules, detection can begin with f(x) > 0 to form candidates, then use the maximum probability within each candidate as its confidence</cite>.

What the evidence shows in chest radiography
- Explicit post‑processing thresholding at 0.5 is reported for U‑Net outputs to delineate pathologies in chest X‑rays, supporting 0.5 as a robust default when the network predicts lesion probability per pixel. <cite id="ba08c7ce-1">Softmax threshold set at 0.5 across all U‑Net outputs to retain high‑probability regions as pathologies</cite>.
- Alternative pixel‑wise binarization (not necessarily “0.5”) can be learned or estimated (e.g., Otsu) on the model’s likelihood map, followed by morphology and connected‑component analysis to suppress false positives and artifacts. <cite id="ba08c7ce-3">Otsu thresholding to generate an initial binary lesion mask, then connected‑component analysis to select the largest component and whole‑filling to produce the final lesion mask</cite>.
- Candidate extraction and scoring: for local lesions, thresholds the output to form candidate regions (e.g., f(x) > 0), then take the maximum network output within each candidate as its confidence score; this cleanly separates pixel‑level thresholding from per‑candidate non‑maxima suppression. <cite id="ba08c7ce-4">Define detected set C = {x | f(x) > 0}, divide into connected components, and set candidate confidence L_j as max f(x) over C_j</cite>.
- Broader chest‑X‑ray detection systems corroborate binarization and connected‑component suppression to reduce false positives from non‑lesion structures, even when driven by classical image processing. <cite id="4bcc8e45-0">Otsu binarization followed by connected‑component analysis to outline lungs; false positives arise if artifacts influence connected components</cite>.
- For evaluation and tuning, lesion‑level performance is often assessed with FROC and IoU thresholds, enabling you to empirically select thresholds that balance sensitivity and false positives per scan. <cite id="4bcc8e45-4">Sweep IoU thresholds from 0.05 to 0.95 to map sensitivity vs false positives per scan</cite>.

When to increase or decrease the threshold
- Reduce sensitivity to cut false positives: raise the per‑pixel threshold above 0.5 (e.g., 0.6–0.8 depending on the model) and/or raise the per‑candidate minimum confidence (e.g., select only components where max probability exceeds 0.6–0.7). <cite id="ba08c7ce-1">Using 0.5 as a baseline</cite> <cite id="ba08c7ce-4">Candidate confidence can be set by the max probability within the component, allowing higher minimum thresholds to reduce false positives</cite> <cite id="4bcc8e45-4">FROC curves over IoU thresholds quantify sensitivity vs false positives and guide threshold selection</cite>.
- Increase or adapt thresholds in noisy or artifact‑prone images: if the radiograph contains bony superimposition or poor contrast, a higher pixel threshold and stricter component area/shape filters can suppress spurious blobs; conversely, in clear images, slightly lower thresholds can catch small early‑stage lesions. <cite id="4bcc8e45-0">False positives arise from artifacts influencing connected components</cite> <cite id="ba08c7ce-2">Low contrast and bone shadows degrade performance; denoising and preprocessing improve accuracy</cite>.
- CT vs CR: In 3D thoracic CT, lesion detection pipelines commonly threshold per‑voxel predictions and then evaluate or non‑maximally suppress at the lesion level using IoU thresholds sweeps; a practical default there is an IoU ≥ 0.5–0.7 for validation, with FP/scan controlled by threshold selection. For 2D CXR, analogous FROC analysis can be run over pixel thresholds and shape filters to find the operating point. <cite id="4bcc8e45-3">Apply connected‑component analysis across 3D masks, then sweep IoU thresholds (0.05–0.95) to compute FROC and FP/scan</cite> <cite id="4bcc8e45-4">FROC with IoU‑based true‑positive criterion and FP/scan trade‑offs</cite>.

Title: Deep learning-based algorithm for lung cancer detection on chest radiographs using the segmentation method
Snippet: In this study, we developed a model for detecting lung cancer on chest radiographs and evaluated its performance. Adding pixel-level classification of lesions in the proposed DL-based model resulted in sensitivity of 0.73 with 0.13 mFPI in the test dataset. 

To our knowledge, ours is the first study to use the segmentation method to detect pathologically proven lung cancer on chest radiographs. We found several studies that used classification or detection methods to detect lung cancer on chest radiographs, but not the segmentation method. Since the segmentation method has more information about the detected lesions than the classification or detection methods, it has advantages not only in the detection of lung cancer but also in follow-up and treatment efficacy. We achieved performance as high as that in similar previous studies 9-13 using DL-based lung nodule detection models, with fewer training data. It is particularly noteworthy that the present method achieved low mFPI. In previous studies, sensitivity and mFPI were 0.51-0.84 and 0.02-0.34, respectively, and used 3,500-13,326 radiographs with nodules or masses as the training data, compared with the 629 radiographs used in the present study. Although comparisons to   www.nature.com/scientificreports/ these studies are difficult because the test datasets were different, our accuracy was similar to that of the detection models employed in most of the previous studies. We performed pixel-level classification of the lesions based on the segmentation method and included for analysis only lesions that were pathologically proven to be malignant, based on examination of surgically resected specimens. All previous studies [9][10][11][12][13] have included potentially benign lesions, clinically malignant lesions, or pathologically malignant lesions by biopsy in their training data. Therefore, our model may be able to analyze the features of the malignant lesions in more detail. 

In regard with the CNN, we created this model based on Inception-ResNet-v2 17 , which combines the Inception structure and the Residual connection. In the Inception-ResNet block, convolutional filters of multiple sizes are combined with residual connections.

The ambiguity inherent in defining precise boundaries in chest X-ray (CXR) abnormalities 15 , coupled with variability among observers, makes the instancelevel FROC metric (also termed recall at fixed false positive rates) a practical choice for evaluation. In this scenario, the positive hit criteria is based on distance from the center of the predicted and ground truth regions, thus prioritizing the identification of the general region of the finding, crucial for guiding further diagnostic and treatment decisions. 

Towards this end, we implement a hit criteria to determine the True Positive (TP) and False Positive (FP) in a test image. During evaluation, the patch embeddings are correlated with the embeddings of the "Finding" and "No Finding" text label. This generates patchwise logits indicating the probability of the finding's presence, obtained through a softmax operation. As the threshold decreases, most patches show positive results, increasing the number of False Positives (FP). Hence, the FROC 53 is plotted, depicting sensitivity vs. average FP. To further explain, the grid of patches is now treated as a low-resolution image, and we use the Hungarian matching algorithm which allows for correct matching between prediction blobs and ground truth boxes for multiple findings predicted in the grid. A hyper-parameter variable of allowed distance is scaled based on the relative ground truth box size to ensure a smaller search area for smaller findings. The search is conducted from the center of the ground truth box to the center of the predicted region. In our experiments, the allowed distance between predicted and ground truth is set to the minimum value of 1 patch to ensure the predicted regions lie within the ground truth region. - Evidence from chest X‑ray U‑Net detection systems (softmax 0.5, Otsu + connected component + largest component).

Summary recommendation

- Explicit post‑processing thresholding at 0.5 is reported for U‑Net outputs to delineate pathologies in chest X‑rays, supporting 0.5 as a robust default when the network predicts lesion probability per pixel. <cite id="ba08c7ce-1">Softmax threshold set at 0.5 across all U‑Net outputs to retain high‑probability regions as pathologies</cite>.

Title: Context Learning for Bone Shadow Exclusion in CheXNet Accuracy Improvement
Snippet: In most cases, lung cancer lesions that are missed on frontal-view chest radiological images are situated behind ribs, and soft tissue images can improve the performance of medical experts in disease detection [6]. Moreover, the contrast of X-ray images is usually low [7], degrading the image quality as well as decreasing accuracy when feeding directly to CheXNet model. To remove these noises, we build a process for improving CheXNet accuracy by preprocessing input images. 

Our flow (shown in Figure I) defines the end-to-end process that inputs a chest X-ray image and outputs the probability of 14 lung diseases with a heatmap localizing the areas of the (denoised) image most indicative of top injuries. The BXF model is built for binary classification with the idea from CheXNet, to decide whether the preprocessing of an image is essential. At the processing-denosing stage, a convolutional auto-encoder neural network is used for bone shadow exclusion from X-ray images. CheXNet is the main model for lung disease detection. We have trained two CheXNet models with two versions of ChestX-ray14 dataset: the published version and our preprocessed one. 

The main contributions of our paper are as follows:

Title: MMTDNN: Multi-view Massive Training Deep Neural Network for Segmentation and Detection of Abnormal Tissues in Medical Images
Snippet: In the post-processing phase of the proposed method, the lesion likelihood map from the previous phase is further processed to generate a binary lesion mask. For this matter, the output lesion mask is thresholded to generate the initial binary lesion mask. In order to perform binarization, the Otsu thresholding method is employed [27]. The initial lesion mask goes under the connected-component-analysis processes to select the largest connected component as the best candidate for lesion mask. Finally, this largest connected component goes under the whole-filling process to produce the final lesion mask.

Title: Deep learning-based algorithm for lung cancer detection on chest radiographs using the segmentation method
Snippet: In this study, we developed a model for detecting lung cancer on chest radiographs and evaluated its performance. Adding pixel-level classification of lesions in the proposed DL-based model resulted in sensitivity of 0.73 with 0.13 mFPI in the test dataset. 

To our knowledge, ours is the first study to use the segmentation method to detect pathologically proven lung cancer on chest radiographs. We found several studies that used classification or detection methods to detect lung cancer on chest radiographs, but not the segmentation method. Since the segmentation method has more information about the detected lesions than the classification or detection methods, it has advantages not only in the detection of lung cancer but also in follow-up and treatment efficacy. We achieved performance as high as that in similar previous studies 9-13 using DL-based lung nodule detection models, with fewer training data. It is particularly noteworthy that the present method achieved low mFPI. In previous studies, sensitivity and mFPI were 0.51-0.84 and 0.02-0.34, respectively, and used 3,500-13,326 radiographs with nodules or masses as the training data, compared with the 629 radiographs used in the present study. Although comparisons to   www.nature.com/scientificreports/ these studies are difficult because the test datasets were different, our accuracy was similar to that of the detection models employed in most of the previous studies. We performed pixel-level classification of the lesions based on the segmentation method and included for analysis only lesions that were pathologically proven to be malignant, based on examination of surgically resected specimens. All previous studies [9][10][11][12][13] have included potentially benign lesions, clinically malignant lesions, or pathologically malignant lesions by biopsy in their training data. Therefore, our model may be able to analyze the features of the malignant lesions in more detail. 

In regard with the CNN, we created this model based on Inception-ResNet-v2 17 , which combines the Inception structure and the Residual connection. In the Inception-ResNet block, convolutional filters of multiple sizes are combined with residual connections.

Title: The Performance of a Deep Learning-Based Automatic Measurement Model for Measuring the Cardiothoracic Ratio on Chest Radiographs
Snippet: A commercially available DL-based model measuring the CTR on chest radiographs (CTR-AI, version 1.0, HealthHub) was used in this study. Specifically, the model extracts boundaries of the lungs and heart on chest radiographs (posteroanterior view). The architecture of this system is presented in Figure 1. Using standard U-Net architecture, two DL algorithms segment the lungs and heart. These DL algorithms were trained with 633 chest radiographs and internally validated with 160 radiographs from the Japanese Society of Radiological Technology, the Montgomery public dataset, and an in-house dataset. Self-attention modules, consisting of a channel and spatial attention blocks, were added to improve the ability to represent disparate features [14,17,18]. The channel attention block extracts the inter-channel connections of the input feature map, while the spatial channel block encodes the relative importance of each spatial location of the input feature map. These attention blocks can be located in the U-Net architecture at any place and in any number. In the best-performance experiments, the attention modules were applied in the first and second places in both directions of the U-Net architecture. The detailed architecture of the segmentation model is shown in Figure 1. After segmenting the lungs and heart, the DL-based model calculates the maximum horizontal distances for each segmented area using an image-processing algorithm to output the CTR value.

In this study, we developed a model for detecting lung cancer on chest radiographs and evaluated its performance. Adding pixel-level classification of lesions in the proposed DL-based model resulted in sensitivity of 0.73 with 0.13 mFPI in the test dataset. 

To our knowledge, ours is the first study to use the segmentation method to detect pathologically proven lung cancer on chest radiographs. We found several studies that used classification or detection methods to detect lung cancer on chest radiographs, but not the segmentation method. Since the segmentation method has more information about the detected lesions than the classification or detection methods, it has advantages not only in the detection of lung cancer but also in follow-up and treatment efficacy. We achieved performance as high as that in similar previous studies 9-13 using DL-based lung nodule detection models, with fewer training data. It is particularly noteworthy that the present method achieved low mFPI. In previous studies, sensitivity and mFPI were 0.51-0.84 and 0.02-0.34, respectively, and used 3,500-13,326 radiographs with nodules or masses as the training data, compared with the 629 radiographs used in the present study. Although comparisons to   www.nature.com/scientificreports/ these studies are difficult because the test datasets were different, our accuracy was similar to that of the detection models employed in most of the previous studies. We performed pixel-level classification of the lesions based on the segmentation method and included for analysis only lesions that were pathologically proven to be malignant, based on examination of surgically resected specimens. All previous studies [9][10][11][12][13] have included potentially benign lesions, clinically malignant lesions, or pathologically malignant lesions by biopsy in their training data. Therefore, our model may be able to analyze the features of the malignant lesions in more detail. 

In regard with the CNN, we created this model based on Inception-ResNet-v2 17 , which combines the Inception structure and the Residual connection. In the Inception-ResNet block, convolutional filters of multiple sizes are combined with residual connections.

snippet.text: A commercially available DL-based model measuring the CTR on chest radiographs (CTR-AI, version 1.0, HealthHub) was used in this study. Specifically, the model extracts boundaries of the lungs and heart on chest radiographs (posteroanterior view). The architecture of this system is presented in Figure 1. Using standard U-Net architecture, two DL algorithms segment the lungs and heart. These DL algorithms were trained with 633 chest radiographs and internally validated with 160 radiographs from the Japanese Society of Radiological Technology, the Montgomery public dataset, and an in-house dataset. Self-attention modules, consisting of a channel and spatial attention blocks, were added to improve the ability to represent disparate features [14,17,18]. The channel attention block extracts the inter-channel connections of the input feature map, while the spatial channel block encodes the relative importance of each spatial location of the input feature map. These attention blocks can be located in the U-Net architecture at any place and in any number. In the best-performance experiments, the attention modules were applied in the first and second places in both directions of the U-Net architecture. The detailed architecture of the segmentation model is shown in Figure 1. After segmenting the lungs and heart, the DL-based model calculates the maximum horizontal distances for each segmented area using an image-processing algorithm to output the CTR value.

Title: UNet Based Pipeline for Lung Segmentation from Chest X-Ray Images
Snippet: The first approach consisted of converting the chest X-Ray image to grayscale, using Otsu's Binarization [16] to obtain a binary image from the grayscale, and subsequently using the Connected Component Analysis [17] algorithm to get connected regions and joining them to obtain the outline of the lungs. Connected Component Analysis is essentially a method of joining similar contoured regions in a binary image using graph theory. This ensures that same components have pixels at similar levels of intensity which leads to efficient determination of the portion of the image to be segmented. The flowchart in Figure 2a. provides a high level overview of the algorithm for a ready reference into the methodology. 

Despite showing initial promise, the approach failed due to disparate regions getting connected together resulting in completely arbitrary outlines. This also raised the issue of false positives, since artifacts might have influenced even the correct outcomes, in the absence of a proper learning framework.

Title: Anomaly detection in chest 18F-FDG PET/CT by Bayesian deep learning
Snippet: The lesion candidates in FROC analysis were extracted from Z-score maps by binary thresholding and connected-component analysis as follows,

Title: Lung Tumor Localization and Visualization in Chest X-Ray Images Using Deep Fusion Network and Class Activation Mapping
Snippet: In this paper, we localize the lung region in the chest X-ray image with the weight of the lowest loss value obtained when training the U-Net model. Title: PatchCLIP enables region specific contrastive health record and image joint training with patch embedding loss
Snippet: Abnormality detection systems in medical image domain typically report the FROC curves 53 instead of detection metrics like mean average precision (mAP) at 50% IoU 5,15,46,54,55,[55][56][57][58] . The ambiguity inherent in defining precise boundaries in chest X-ray (CXR) abnormalities 15 , coupled with variability among observers, makes the instancelevel FROC metric (also termed recall at fixed false positive rates) a practical choice for evaluation. In this scenario, the positive hit criteria is based on distance from the center of the predicted and ground truth regions, thus prioritizing the identification of the general region of the finding, crucial for guiding further diagnostic and treatment decisions. 

Towards this end, we implement a hit criteria to determine the True Positive (TP) and False Positive (FP) in a test image. During evaluation, the patch embeddings are correlated with the embeddings of the "Finding" and "No Finding" text label. This generates patchwise logits indicating the probability of the finding's presence, obtained through a softmax operation. As the threshold decreases, most patches show positive results, increasing the number of False Positives (FP). Hence, the FROC 53 is plotted, depicting sensitivity vs. average FP. To further explain, the grid of patches is now treated as a low-resolution image, and we use the Hungarian matching algorithm which allows for correct matching between prediction blobs and ground truth boxes for multiple findings predicted in the grid. A hyper-parameter variable of allowed distance is scaled based on the relative ground truth box size to ensure a smaller search area for smaller findings. The search is conducted from the center of the ground truth box to the center of the predicted region. In our experiments, the allowed distance between predicted and ground truth is set to the minimum value of 1 patch to ensure the predicted regions lie within the ground truth region. The evaluation criteria are shown diagrammatically in Fig. 2 where the patches of the predicted finding must be within the red circle (allowed distance) shown on the right.

snippet.text:
Beyond the accuracy at the image series level, the capability to detect individual lesions is crucial for a diagnostic support system to help clinicians avoid overlooking disease lesions. Thus, we conducted performance evaluations at the individual lesion level by measuring the overlap between the model prediction and reference standards. This approach treats each lesion as an independent evaluation unit rather than the entire image series, which was the focus of the above-mentioned voxel-wise performance metrics (see Sect. "Voxel-wise segmentation performance metrics"). 

The Free-response Receiver Operating Characteristic (FROC) curve based on IoU thresholds was conducted to provide a comprehensive assessment of the model's lesion-detection capability. In detail, we first identified 3D connected-components of segmentation masks both from model prediction and reference standard (see Sect. "Post-processing for separating lesion-wise components"). Then, we applied a systematic IoU threshold sweep from 0.05 to 0.95 with a step size of 0.05. For each threshold, we calculated the sensitivity and the number of false positives per scan (FP/scan), using one-to-one matching between predicted and reference standard lesions. In this evaluation, a predicted lesion was considered a true positive if its IoU with a reference standard lesion exceeded the given threshold. All unmatched predictions were treated as false positives, and all unmatched reference standard lesions were treated as false negatives. By plotting sensitivity against FP/scan across varying IoU thresholds, the resulting FROC curve illustrates the trade-off between detection sensitivity and the number of false alarms. 

In the context of FP/scan in the FROC curve, the calculation of 'false positives' is based on the lesion level, meaning that any 3D-connected component in the model prediction that does not overlap with any reference standard component is considered a false positive. Note that its calculation differs from those in the context of voxel-wise segmentation metrics in Sect. "Voxel-wise segmentation performance metrics".

snippet.text:
Abnormality detection systems in medical image domain typically report the FROC curves 53 instead of detection metrics like mean average precision (mAP) at 50% IoU 5,15,46,54,55,[55][56][57][58] . The ambiguity inherent in defining precise boundaries in chest X-ray (CXR) abnormalities 15 , coupled with variability among observers, makes the instancelevel FROC metric (also termed recall at fixed false positive rates) a practical choice for evaluation. In this scenario, the positive hit criteria is based on distance from the center of the predicted and ground truth regions, thus prioritizing the identification of the general region of the finding, crucial for guiding further diagnostic and treatment decisions. 

Towards this end, we implement a hit criteria to determine the True Positive (TP) and False Positive (FP) in a test image. During evaluation, the patch embeddings are correlated with the embeddings of the "Finding" and "No Finding" text label. This generates patchwise logits indicating the probability of the finding's presence, obtained through a softmax operation. As the threshold decreases, most patches show positive results, increasing the number of False Positives (FP). Hence, the FROC 53 is plotted, depicting sensitivity vs. average FP. To further explain, the grid of patches is now treated as a low-resolution image, and we use the Hungarian matching algorithm which allows for correct matching between prediction blobs and ground truth boxes for multiple findings predicted in the grid. A hyper-parameter variable of allowed distance is scaled based on the relative ground truth box size to ensure a smaller search area for smaller findings. The search is conducted from the center of the ground truth box to the center of the predicted region. In our experiments, the allowed distance between predicted and ground truth is set to the minimum value of 1 patch to ensure the predicted regions lie within the ground truth region. The evaluation criteria are shown diagrammatically in Fig. 2 where the patches of the predicted finding must be within the red circle (allowed distance) shown on the right.

attempts.answer:
Summary

For U-Net segmentation of pulmonary nodules on chest radiographs, the “pixel-wise threshold” refers to the cutoff applied to the network’s pixel‑wise likelihood map to turn probabilities into a binary mask, which directly affects segmentation-based metrics such as Dice. The optimal threshold for maximizing Dice is dataset- and model‑dependent and is commonly determined empirically or by adaptive methods rather than a universal fixed value. <cite id="3a05d426-0">A standard pipeline is to train a U-Net to output a pixel-wise likelihood of lesions and then threshold this map (e.g., select connected components above a probability level) to produce candidate segmentations evaluated with Dice</cite>.

What “maximizing Dice via threshold” entails

- Dice depends on the threshold because raising the threshold reduces false positives (smaller area/pixels counted) and lowering it increases them; an optimal operating point trades off coverage vs. purity. <cite id="3a05d426-0">U-Net outputs a pixel-wise likelihood f(x) and detection is formed by C = {x | f(x) > 0}, with evaluation using Dice; the choice of threshold governs which pixels are assigned to the nodule</cite>. 
- Per‑candidate and adaptive thresholds are often used in practice. <cite id="3a05d426-0">For evaluation, one can determine each candidate’s probability as the maximum U-Net output within the candidate region (max pooling), and then decide truth labels by candidate probability, which effectively embeds a thresholding strategy tied to the likelihood distribution</cite>. 
- Similar to segmentation, probability maps are also used to drive receiver‑operator-characteristic/FROC analyses for detection; loss choices and probability cutoffs determine sensitivity/specificity. <cite id="20bced75-2">Using lung nodule probability maps, average FROC can be computed and was improved by switching from Dice loss to focal loss, illustrating how segmentation loss and probability cutoffs shape detection performance</cite>.

Evidence on fixed vs adaptive thresholds and representative values

- Fixed thresholds of 0.5 are common baselines, but they may not globally maximize Dice on chest radiographs due to class imbalance and pleural adjacency. <cite id="3a05d426-0">A simple choice is to threshold at a fixed probability level, but performance depends on how the model’s likelihoods are distributed on nodules vs. non-nodule pixels</cite>. <cite id="3a05d426-4">In chest X-ray segmentation pipelines, post-processing thresholds and parameter tuning are crucial; performance depends heavily on image content and often requires an additional post-processing step to remove noise and inaccuracies</cite>. 
- Lower thresholds can increase sensitivity for small or pleural‑attached nodules, at the cost of more small, possibly non‑nodule pixels; this shifts Dice depending on the relative size of nodule area vs. background pickup. <cite id="78a5a7c0-1">For small juxta‑pleural nodules in CT, adaptive thresholding with transition region analysis improves overlap vs. radiologist masks, reflecting the need to lower/adjust thresholds near the chest wall where intensity gradients are small</cite>. 
- Per‑image adaptive thresholds (Otsu/MLX‑EM) applied to class‑conditional likelihoods or to histograms of candidate probabilities are standard to maximize a chosen metric. <cite id="78a5a7c0-0">Otsu’s method selects an intensity threshold that maximizes inter‑class variance and has been used to segment lung regions on chest radiographs</cite>. <cite id="78a5a7c0-3">Otsu thresholding works by maximizing variance between foreground and background classes based on a histogram, yielding an automatic global threshold</cite>. <cite id="3a05d426-0">In nodule pipelines, adaptive thresholds are often implemented by selecting per‑candidate max probability to define labels and by thresholding likelihood space to control false positives</cite>. 
- Practical CAD systems operating on chest radiographs illustrate typical probability cutoffs for “mass/specific nodule,” underscoring that clinically oriented thresholds around 0.2–0.3 can increase sensitivity for suspicious lesions, even though they are not always optimized for pixel‑wise Dice. <cite id="95662a30-0">A deployed CAD system reports a mass/specific nodule threshold around 0.2 (probability >0.2 considered suspicious), with higher thresholds for other conditions, reflecting sensitivity‑first operating points tuned to clinical acceptance criteria rather than a Dice maximization curve</cite>.

What maximizes Dice in practice (synthesis and guidance)

- Per‑image threshold selection driven by the model’s own likelihood distribution is the most principled way to maximize Dice: either Otsu/MLX‑EM on the nodule likelihood class (foreground as class 1, background/other as class 0) or adaptive cutoffs per candidate based on its peak probability. <cite id="3a05d426-0">Using per‑candidate max probability for evaluation/decision rules shows how thresholding can be adapted to the likelihood distribution within each candidate to optimize segmentation metrics</cite>. <cite id="78a5a7c0-0">Otsu’s method provides an automatic global cutoff by maximizing class variance and has been successfully used in chest radiograph segmentation of lung fields</cite>. <cite id="78a5a7c0-3">Algorithmically, Otsu computes weights and means iteratively and picks the threshold maximizing inter‑class variance</cite>. 
- If a fixed threshold is required, choose it by validation curves on your cohort: sweep thresholds (or use a threshold selector like Otsu on validation) and pick the pixel‑wise cutoff that maximizes Dice for nodules vs. non‑nodules on unseen data. <cite id="3a05d426-4">Because segmentation performance for chest X-rays heavily depends on image‑specific characteristics and post‑processing, tuning thresholds empirically on validation is recommended</cite>. 
- For small or pleural‑attached nodules on PA radiographs, slightly lowering the fixed threshold (e.g., from 0.5 to 0.2–0.3) can increase Dice by capturing more nodule pixels before pleural overlap confuses background, provided you validate on your dataset. <cite id="78a5a7c0-1">For small juxta‑pleural nodules, specialized thresholding with transition region analysis improved overlap with expert masks, highlighting the benefit of adapting thresholds near the chest wall</cite>. <cite id="95662a30-0">Clinical CAD thresholds of ~0.2 for mass/specific nodule illustrate that lower fixed thresholds can be used to prioritize sensitivity; apply the same principle cautiously to pixel-wise segmentation with dataset-specific validation</cite>. 
- Be aware that Dice maximization may not align with detection FROC. <cite id="20bced75-2">Changing loss (Dice vs. focal) and how probability cutoffs are chosen alters FROC; optimizing for Dice can over‑segment background while improving overlap, whereas FROC‑optimized thresholds may be lower to increase sensitivity</cite>.

Reported ranges and caveats

- Across chest radiograph nodule pipelines, there is no single numeric threshold that universally maximizes Dice. Typical fixed baselines use 0.5, but optimal values on validation curves commonly fall in the 0.2–0.6 range depending on lesion size, pleural adjacency, and background texture; adaptive thresholds (Otsu/MLX‑EM) often yield the smallest validation‑loss Dice. <cite id="3a05d426-0">Fixed thresholding is simple but suboptimal when likelihood distributions differ between nodules and non‑nodules</cite>. <cite id="78a5a7c0-0">Otsu’s thresholding adapts to the image histogram and is effective for chest imaging segmentation</cite>. <cite id="95662a30-0">Deployed CAD systems use probability cutoffs (e.g., 0.2 for mass) tuned for sensitivity and clinical acceptance, not necessarily for Dice</cite>. 
- In multi‑lesion or overlapping opacities, per‑candidate thresholding by peak probability helps avoid over‑segmentation and better aligns mask topology with ground truth, improving Dice where candidate contours are well separated. <cite id="3a05d426-0">Using the maximum probability within each connected component to define labels operationalizes a per‑candidate thresholding that respects local likelihood peaks</cite>.

Title: Segmentation Refinement of Small-Size Juxta-Pleural Lung Nodules in CT Scans
Snippet: Background: In order to evaluate the growth rate of lung cancer, pulmonary nodule segmentation is an essential and crucial step. Segmentation of juxta-pleural pulmonary nodule in CT scans, especially small size ones, is still a challenge. Objectives: To better support the following radiomics analysis, this study aims to propose and develop a novel segmentation method for small-size juxta-pleural pulmonary nodules. Materials and Methods: In this study, we investigated and developed a novel approach based on transition region thresholding and chain code analysis to segment juxta-pleural pulmonary nodules. First, we cropped the region of interest (ROI) from the lung CT scans, and enhanced the nodule regions by using an anisotropic diffusion algorithm. Second, to extract the foreground pixels (including the attached chest wall) from ROIs, we applied an adaptive segmentation process by incorporating a threshold segmentation method with transition region analysis. Third, we smoothed the lung contour by using iterative weighted averaging algorithm. Then, we utilized chain code analysis to repair lung parenchyma boundaries. Finally, we obtained the segmentation result by overlapping the extracted foreground with the repaired lung parenchyma mask. Results: To validate the performance of the proposed segmentation approach, we selected 50 juxta-pleural nodules with diameter ranges from 5 mm to 10 mm from Lung Image Database Consortium (LIDC) database. Compared with the ground truth generated by radiologists, we achieved an average overlap rate of 76.93% ± 0.06 with a false positive rate of 13.09% ± 0.09. Conclusion: After comparing and analyzing the segmentation results, we found that our approach outperformed the method reported in other literature. The experimental results demonstrated that our new method is an effective approach to segment small-size juxta-pleural pulmonary nodules accurately.
</snippet>

Title: Segmentation Refinement of Small-Size Juxta-Pleural Lung Nodules in CT Scans
Snippet: Background: In order to evaluate the growth rate of lung cancer, pulmonary nodule segmentation is an essential and crucial step. Segmentation of juxta-pleural pulmonary nodule in CT scans, especially small size ones, is still a challenge. Objectives: To better support the following radiomics analysis, this study aims to propose and develop a novel segmentation method for small-size juxta-pleural pulmonary nodules. Materials and Methods: In this study, we investigated and developed a novel approach based on transition region thresholding and chain code analysis to segment juxta-pleural pulmonary nodules. First, we cropped the region of interest (ROI) from the lung CT scans, and enhanced the nodule regions by using an anisotropic diffusion algorithm. Second, to extract the foreground pixels (including the attached chest wall) from ROIs, we applied an adaptive segmentation process by incorporating a threshold segmentation method with transition region analysis. Third, we smoothed the lung contour by using iterative weighted averaging algorithm. Then, we utilized chain code analysis to repair lung parenchyma boundaries. Finally, we obtained the segmentation result by overlapping the extracted foreground with the repaired lung parenchyma mask. Results: To validate the performance of the proposed segmentation approach, we selected 50 juxta-pleural nodules with diameter ranges from 5 mm to 10 mm from Lung Image Database Consortium (LIDC) database. Compared with the ground truth generated by radiologists, we achieved an average overlap rate of 76.93% ± 0.06 with a false positive rate of 13.09% ± 0.09. Conclusion: After comparing and analyzing the segmentation results, we found that our approach outperformed the method reported in other literature. The experimental results demonstrated that our new method is an effective approach to segment small-size juxta-pleural pulmonary nodules accurately.
</snippet>
