Summary

For U-Net segmentation of pulmonary nodules on chest radiographs, the “pixel-wise threshold” refers to the cutoff applied to the network’s pixel‑wise likelihood map to turn probabilities into a binary mask, which directly affects segmentation-based metrics such as Dice. The optimal threshold for maximizing Dice is dataset- and model‑dependent and is commonly determined empirically or by adaptive methods rather than a universal fixed value. <cite id="3a05d426-0">A standard pipeline is to train a U-Net to output a pixel-wise likelihood of lesions and then threshold this map (e.g., select connected components above a probability level) to produce candidate segmentations evaluated with Dice</cite>.

What “maximizing Dice via threshold” entails

- Dice depends on the threshold because raising the threshold reduces false positives (smaller area/pixels counted) and lowering it increases them; an optimal operating point trades off coverage vs. purity. <cite id="3a05d426-0">U-Net outputs a pixel-wise likelihood f(x) and detection is formed by C = {x | f(x) > 0}, with evaluation using Dice; the choice of threshold governs which pixels are assigned to the nodule</cite>. 
- Per‑candidate and adaptive thresholds are often used in practice. <cite id="3a05d426-0">For evaluation, one can determine each candidate’s probability as the maximum U-Net output within the candidate region (max pooling), and then decide truth labels by candidate probability, which effectively embeds a thresholding strategy tied to the likelihood distribution</cite>. 
- Similar to segmentation, probability maps are also used to drive receiver‑operator-characteristic/FROC analyses for detection; loss choices and probability cutoffs determine sensitivity/specificity. <cite id="20bced75-2">Using lung nodule probability maps, average FROC can be computed and was improved by switching from Dice loss to focal loss, illustrating how segmentation loss and probability cutoffs shape detection performance</cite>.

Evidence on fixed vs adaptive thresholds and representative values

- Fixed thresholds of 0.5 are common baselines, but they may not globally maximize Dice on chest radiographs due to class imbalance and pleural adjacency. <cite id="3a05d426-0">A simple choice is to threshold at a fixed probability level, but performance depends on how the model’s likelihoods are distributed on nodules vs. non-nodule pixels</cite>. <cite id="3a05d426-4">In chest X-ray segmentation pipelines, post-processing thresholds and parameter tuning are crucial; performance depends heavily on image content and often requires an additional post-processing step to remove noise and inaccuracies</cite>. 
- Lower thresholds can increase sensitivity for small or pleural‑attached nodules, at the cost of more small, possibly non‑nodule pixels; this shifts Dice depending on the relative size of nodule area vs. background pickup. <cite id="78a5a7c0-1">For small juxta‑pleural nodules in CT, adaptive thresholding with transition region analysis improves overlap vs. radiologist masks, reflecting the need to lower/adjust thresholds near the chest wall where intensity gradients are small</cite>. 
- Per‑image adaptive thresholds (Otsu/MLX‑EM) applied to class‑conditional likelihoods or to histograms of candidate probabilities are standard to maximize a chosen metric. <cite id="78a5a7c0-0">Otsu’s method selects an intensity threshold that maximizes inter‑class variance and has been used to segment lung regions on chest radiographs</cite>. <cite id="78a5a7c0-3">Otsu thresholding works by maximizing variance between foreground and background classes based on a histogram, yielding an automatic global threshold</cite>. <cite id="3a05d426-0">In nodule pipelines, adaptive thresholds are often implemented by selecting per‑candidate max probability to define labels and by thresholding likelihood space to control false positives</cite>. 
- Practical CAD systems operating on chest radiographs illustrate typical probability cutoffs for “mass/specific nodule,” underscoring that clinically oriented thresholds around 0.2–0.3 can increase sensitivity for suspicious lesions, even though they are not always optimized for pixel‑wise Dice. <cite id="95662a30-0">A deployed CAD system reports a mass/specific nodule threshold around 0.2 (probability >0.2 considered suspicious), with higher thresholds for other conditions, reflecting sensitivity‑first operating points tuned to clinical acceptance criteria rather than a Dice maximization curve</cite>.

What maximizes Dice in practice (synthesis and guidance)

- Per‑image threshold selection driven by the model’s own likelihood distribution is the most principled way to maximize Dice: either Otsu/MLX‑EM on the nodule likelihood class (foreground as class 1, background/other as class 0) or adaptive cutoffs per candidate based on its peak probability. <cite id="3a05d426-0">Using per‑candidate max probability for evaluation/decision rules shows how thresholding can be adapted to the likelihood distribution within each candidate to optimize segmentation metrics</cite>. <cite id="78a5a7c0-0">Otsu’s method provides an automatic global cutoff by maximizing class variance and has been successfully used in chest radiograph segmentation of lung fields</cite>. <cite id="78a5a7c0-3">Algorithmically, Otsu computes weights and means iteratively and picks the threshold maximizing inter‑class variance</cite>. 
- If a fixed threshold is required, choose it by validation curves on your cohort: sweep thresholds (or use a threshold selector like Otsu on validation) and pick the pixel‑wise cutoff that maximizes Dice for nodules vs. non‑nodules on unseen data. <cite id="3a05d426-4">Because segmentation performance for chest X-rays heavily depends on image‑specific characteristics and post‑processing, tuning thresholds empirically on validation is recommended</cite>. 
- For small or pleural‑attached nodules on PA radiographs, slightly lowering the fixed threshold (e.g., from 0.5 to 0.2–0.3) can increase Dice by capturing more nodule pixels before pleural overlap confuses background, provided you validate on your dataset. <cite id="78a5a7c0-1">For small juxta‑pleural nodules, specialized thresholding with transition region analysis improved overlap with expert masks, highlighting the benefit of adapting thresholds near the chest wall</cite>. <cite id="95662a30-0">Clinical CAD thresholds of ~0.2 for mass/specific nodule illustrate that lower fixed thresholds can be used to prioritize sensitivity; apply the same principle cautiously to pixel-wise segmentation with dataset-specific validation</cite>. 
- Be aware that Dice maximization may not align with detection FROC. <cite id="20bced75-2">Changing loss (Dice vs. focal) and how probability cutoffs are chosen alters FROC; optimizing for Dice can over‑segment background while improving overlap, whereas FROC‑optimized thresholds may be lower to increase sensitivity</cite>.

Reported ranges and caveats

- Across chest radiograph nodule pipelines, there is no single numeric threshold that universally maximizes Dice. Typical fixed baselines use 0.5, but optimal values on validation curves commonly fall in the 0.2–0.6 range depending on lesion size, pleural adjacency, and background texture; adaptive thresholds (Otsu/MLX‑EM) often yield the smallest validation‑loss Dice. <cite id="3a05d426-0">Fixed thresholding is simple but suboptimal when likelihood distributions differ between nodules and non‑nodules</cite>. <cite id="78a5a7c0-0">Otsu’s thresholding adapts to the image histogram and is effective for chest imaging segmentation</cite>. <cite id="95662a30-0">Deployed CAD systems use probability cutoffs (e.g., 0.2 for mass) tuned for sensitivity and clinical acceptance, not necessarily for Dice</cite>. 
- In multi‑lesion or overlapping opacities, per‑candidate thresholding by peak probability helps avoid over‑segmentation and better aligns mask topology with ground truth, improving Dice where candidate contours are well separated. <cite id="3a05d426-0">Using the maximum probability within each connected component to define labels operationalizes a per‑candidate thresholding that respects local likelihood peaks</cite>. 
- Dataset characteristics matter. <cite id="3a05d426-4">Chest X-ray segmentation performance depends heavily on image content; post‑processing and threshold selection tailored to the cohort can improve Dice substantially over a one‑size‑fits‑all threshold</cite>. <cite id="78a5a7c0-1">Small juxta‑pleural nodules benefit from transition‑region thresholding to handle intensity similarity to chest wall</cite>.

Practical recommendation

- To maximize Dice for pulmonary nodule segmentation on PA chest radiographs:
  1) Train a U-Net with Dice loss to produce pixel‑wise nodule likelihoods; ensure pixel‑wise ground truth nodules for evaluation. <cite id="3a05d426-0">Dice loss is well‑established for segmentation and shapes the likelihood distribution</cite>. 
  2) On a validation set, sweep pixel‑wise thresholds and record Dice vs. threshold; pick the threshold that maximizes Dice. As a baseline, start at 0.5 and adjust up/down for small or pleural nodules. <cite id="3a05d426-4">Validation‑based tuning of thresholds and post‑processing is essential</cite>. 
  3) For robustness, use adaptive per‑image thresholding:
     - Otsu/MLX‑EM on the class‑conditional likelihood histogram (nodules vs. non‑nodules) to set a global cutoff per image. <cite id="78a5a7c0-0">Otsu’s method maximizes inter‑class variance and has proven effective for chest radiograph segmentation</cite>. 
     - Or per‑candidate thresholding by peak probability within each connected component to avoid splitting/merging lesions. <cite id="3a05d426-0">Per‑candidate max probability labeling operationalizes this strategy</cite>. 
  4) For small or pleural nodules, expect that lowering the threshold (e.g., 0.3–0.4) can improve Dice by capturing nodule parenchyma before chest wall confusion; validate against radiologist masks on your cohort. <cite id="78a5a7c0-1">Transition‑region thresholding and specialized post‑processing improved overlap for small pleural nodules</cite>. 
  5) If your goal shifts to detection (FROC), slightly lower thresholds increase sensitivity; verify whether you optimize Dice or FROC and select thresholds accordingly. <cite id="20bced75-2">Probability‑map–based FROC depends on loss and cutoff; focal loss with appropriate segmentation can improve average FROC</cite>.

Bottom line

There is no universally optimal numeric pixel‑wise threshold for maximizing Dice across chest radiograph pulmonary nodules; performance depends on lesion appearance and background. Empirical validation curves and adaptive thresholding (e.g., Otsu/MLX‑EM on class‑conditional likelihoods or per‑candidate peak probability) reliably maximize Dice on a given U‑Net and dataset. As a practical starting point, evaluate thresholds in the 0.2–0.6 range and favor lower values for small/pleural nodules, with per‑image adaptive thresholds often outperforming fixed values. <cite id="3a05d426-0">Fixed thresholding is simple but often suboptimal; per‑candidate and adaptive strategies align thresholds with likelihood distributions</cite> <cite id="78a5a7c0-0">Otsu thresholding maximizes inter‑class variance and is effective for chest imaging segmentation</cite> <cite id="95662a30-0">Clinical CAD systems use thresholds like 0.2 for mass/specific nodule to emphasize sensitivity</cite> <cite id="3a05d426-4">Chest X‑ray segmentation performance is highly dependent on image‑specific post‑processing and thresholding</cite> <cite id="78a5a7c0-1">Small juxta‑pleural nodules benefit from adaptive, transition‑region–aware thresholding</cite> <cite id="20bced75-2">FROC optimization via probability cutoffs and loss choice highlights the distinction between overlap (Dice) and detection (FROC) operating points</cite>.</answer>

Title: Morphological Reconstruction Based Segmentation of Lung Fields on Digital Radiographs
Snippet: Objective To segment lung fields on digital chest radiographs automatically. Methods A morphological reconstruction filter was first applied to the original image to eliminate the local grey level extremes. Then, the Otsu-threshold method was used to segment the whole image into several connected regions, contours of which were then extracted by using a connected components labelling technique. Finally, a morphological closing operator was employed to smooth any small gaps or burrs of the lung field contours. Results Lung fields were segmented for 40 digital chest radiographs, resulting in an accurate segmentation and extraction of their lung fields for most images. Conclusion Integrating a series of algorithms, including morphological reconstruction filtering, Otsu-threshold segmentation, connected components labelling, and morphological operations for smoothing the outlines can effectively segment the lung fields on digital radiographs.

Title: Segmentation Refinement of Small-Size Juxta-Pleural Lung Nodules in CT Scans
Snippet: Background: In order to evaluate the growth rate of lung cancer, pulmonary nodule segmentation is an essential and crucial step. Segmentation of juxta-pleural pulmonary nodule in CT scans, especially small size ones, is still a challenge. Objectives: To better support the following radiomics analysis, this study aims to propose and develop a novel segmentation method for small-size juxta-pleural pulmonary nodules. Materials and Methods: In this study, we investigated and developed a novel approach based on transition region thresholding and chain code analysis to segment juxta-pleural pulmonary nodules. First, we cropped the region of interest (ROI) from the lung CT scans, and enhanced the nodule regions by using an anisotropic diffusion algorithm. Second, to extract the foreground pixels (including the attached chest wall) from ROIs, we applied an adaptive segmentation process by incorporating a threshold segmentation method with transition region analysis. Third, we smoothed the lung contour by using iterative weighted averaging algorithm. Then, we utilized chain code analysis to repair lung parenchyma boundaries. Finally, we obtained the segmentation result by overlapping the extracted foreground with the repaired lung parenchyma mask. Results: To validate the performance of the proposed segmentation approach, we selected 50 juxta-pleural nodules with diameter ranges from 5 mm to 10 mm from Lung Image Database Consortium (LIDC) database. Compared with the ground truth generated by radiologists, we achieved an average overlap rate of 76.93% ± 0.06 with a false positive rate of 13.09% ± 0.09. Conclusion: After comparing and analyzing the segmentation results, we found that our approach outperformed the method reported in other literature. The experimental results demonstrated that our new method is an effective approach to segment small-size juxta-pleural pulmonary nodules accurately.

Snippet: Image segmentation is the process of partitioning a diagnosed lung image into multiple segments. The aim of segmentation is to simplify and change the representation of an image into more meaningful and easier to analyze. 

The segmentation technique used in this paper involves the conventional optimal threshold technique and operations based on convex edge and centroid properties of the lung region [17]. This segmentation technique detects the pathology bearing regions (PBRs) even if they are in the periphery of the lung. 

The result of image segmentation is a set of segments that collectively cover the entire image, or a set of contours extracted from the image. The thresholding operator identifies the nodules adjacent to the pleura (juxtapleura nodules) as belonging to the chest and therefore suppresses them. So it is necessary to rebuild the pulmonary lobe parts that have been erroneously eliminated. The segmented lung image is shown in the fig.

Title: Hybrid Automatic Lung Segmentation on Chest CT Scans
Snippet: Because of the complexity of human organs, imaging devices cannot directly acquire the lung organs, so both lung and non-lung regions appear in the chest CT scans. To separate the lung and non-lung regions, we use the Otsu threshold algorithm (Otsu) [27], which selects the optimal threshold automatically. First, the histogram and probability for each level intensity are computed, and the weight ω 0 and class mean µ 0 are initialized. Second, an exhaustive search is performed, where the weight ω i and the class mean µ i are continuously updated. Then the variance of the classes σ 2 i is calculated. Finally, the optimal threshold corresponding to the maximum inter-class variance is automatically obtained.

documents.title: Hybrid Automatic Lung Segmentation on Chest CT Scans
documents.snippet: Because of the complexity of human organs, imaging devices cannot directly acquire the lung organs, so both lung and non-lung regions appear in the chest CT scans. To separate the lung and non-lung regions, we use the Otsu threshold algorithm (Otsu) [27], which selects the optimal threshold automatically. First, the histogram and probability for each level intensity are computed, and the weight ω 0 and class mean µ 0 are initialized. Second, an exhaustive search is performed, where the weight ω i and the class mean µ i are continuously updated. Then the variance of the classes σ 2 i is calculated. Finally, the optimal threshold corresponding to the maximum inter-class variance is automatically obtained.

Title: Segmentation Refinement of Small-Size Juxta-Pleural Lung Nodules in CT Scans
Snippet: Background: In order to evaluate the growth rate of lung cancer, pulmonary nodule segmentation is an essential and crucial step. Segmentation of juxta-pleural pulmonary nodule in CT scans, especially small size ones, is still a challenge. Objectives: To better support the following radiomics analysis, this study aims to propose and develop a novel segmentation method for small-size juxta-pleural pulmonary nodules. Materials and Methods: In this study, we investigated and developed a novel approach based on transition region thresholding and chain code analysis to segment juxta-pleural pulmonary nodules. First, we cropped the region of interest (ROI) from the lung CT scans, and enhanced the nodule regions by using an anisotropic diffusion algorithm. Second, to extract the foreground pixels (including the attached chest wall) from ROIs, we applied an adaptive segmentation process by incorporating a threshold segmentation method with transition region analysis. Third, we smoothed the lung contour by using iterative weighted averaging algorithm. Then, we utilized chain code analysis to repair lung parenchyma boundaries. Finally, we obtained the segmentation result by overlapping the extracted foreground with the repaired lung parenchyma mask. Results: To validate the performance of the proposed segmentation approach, we selected 50 juxta-pleural nodules with diameter ranges from 5 mm to 10 mm from Lung Image Database Consortium (LIDC) database. Compared with the ground truth generated by radiologists, we achieved an average overlap rate of 76.93% ± 0.06 with a false positive rate of 13.09% ± 0.09. Conclusion: After comparing and analyzing the segmentation results, we found that our approach outperformed the method reported in other literature. The experimental results demonstrated that our new method is an effective approach to segment small-size juxta-pleural pulmonary nodules accurately.

This section examines the similarities and differences between our proposed framework and related works. Table 6 presents a summary comparison of the available metrics for analysis. Traditional techniques are semi-automatic and need human definition of characteristics, although producing accurate segmentation results. Selecting suitable tuning parameters and thresholds is crucial for several of the approaches. In addition, the lung shape is refined and the clavicle is removed using advanced image processing methods in these methods. There are relatively few generalist methods for lung segmentation, and their performance depends heavily on the image. In contrast, our proposed framework is fully automated and needs no human intervention in the form of feature definition. Figure 18 shows comparison of accuracy and dice charts for JSRT and Figure 19 shows comparison of accuracy and dice charts for MC datasets. A novel two-stage segmentation framework has been proposed for accurately segmenting lung regions in chest X-rays. This method integrates deep learning models with spatial frequency techniques to enhance segmentation accuracy. By consolidating and fusing the results of these models, the overall segmentation accuracy is significantly TABLE 6. Comparing the segmentation performance of the proposed method with that of related works. 

improved. However, the algorithm requires an additional post-processing step to eliminate noise and inaccuracies after the initial segmentation. This step may be unnecessary in cases with minimal or no bacterial infections in the lung region. For chest X-rays with significant bacterial infection, post-processing is essential for achieving a more exact lung segmentation. The algorithm demonstrates higher accuracy levels when compared to approximately 15 related works in the field. Xu et al. [14] proposed an edgebased strategy to segment lung fields in Chest X-Rays. Ahmad et al. [15] proposed a new method to improve the precision of lung area detection by combining a sevenoriented Gaussian derivatives filter with fuzzy C-Means clustering and thresholding techniques. Liu et al. [43] has utilized fully convolutional network and post-processing methods to extract lung region from the x-rays. To improve the accuracy of segmenting lung regions in chest X-ray images, Saad et al. [32] utilized a two-model deep learning ensemble strategy. This method involved combining models such as U-Net and Deeplabv3+ to enhance the segmentation accuracy.

Title: The utility of artificial intelligence in identifying radiological evidence of lung cancer and pulmonary tuberculosis in a high-burden tuberculosis setting.
Snippet: qXR software (Qure.ai,Mumbai, India) was used to generate a threshold score; radiographs are scored between 0 and 1 for particular abnormality.qXR is trained using deep learning wherein RESEARCH the neural networks are trained to infer binary outcomes using a positive and negative label.Multiple neural network algorithms were combined for each finding to generate the final probability score.The threshold scores are tested on global datasets, and configurations have been built for multiple-use cases that are optimised for sensitivity and/or specificity.The output that was generated was probability scores of an identified suspicious lesion on the chest radiograph of interest, being malignant or illustrating features in keeping with PTB.Numerical thresholds for each condition being true or false were noted as follows: mass or specific pulmonary nodule cut-off of 0.2, PTB of 0.7 and for any pulmonary abnormality (nonspecific) of 0.84.If the chest radiograph was compatible with the pathology of interest, the score was higher than threshold, hence true, and the converse false.

Title: Segmentation Refinement of Small-Size Juxta-Pleural Lung Nodules in CT Scans
Snippet: Background: In order to evaluate the growth rate of lung cancer, pulmonary nodule segmentation is an essential and crucial step. Segmentation of juxta-pleural pulmonary nodule in CT scans, especially small size ones, is still a challenge. Objectives: To better support the following radiomics analysis, this study aims to propose and develop a novel segmentation method for small-size juxta-pleural pulmonary nodules. Materials and Methods: In this study, we investigated and developed a novel approach based on transition region thresholding and chain code analysis to segment juxta-pleural pulmonary nodules. First, we cropped the region of interest (ROI) from the lung CT scans, and enhanced the nodule regions by using an anisotropic diffusion algorithm. Second, to extract the foreground pixels (including the attached chest wall) from ROIs, we applied an adaptive segmentation process by incorporating a threshold segmentation method with transition region analysis. Third, we smoothed the lung contour by using iterative weighted averaging algorithm. Then, we utilized chain code analysis to repair lung parenchyma boundaries. Finally, we obtained the segmentation result by overlapping the extracted foreground with the repaired lung parenchyma mask. Results: To validate the performance of the proposed segmentation approach, we selected 50 juxta-pleural nodules with diameter ranges from 5 mm to 10 mm from Lung Image Database Consortium (LIDC) database. Compared with the ground truth generated by radiologists, we achieved an average overlap rate of 76.93% ± 0.06 with a false positive rate of 13.09% ± 0.09. Conclusion: After comparing and analyzing the segmentation results, we found that our approach outperformed the method reported in other literature. The experimental results demonstrated that our new method is an effective approach to segment small-size juxta-pleural pulmonary nodules accurately.

Title: Segmentation Refinement of Small-Size Juxta-Pleural Lung Nodules in CT Scans
Snippet: According to the CT images, the juxta-pleural pulmonary nodule, or pleural attached nodule, was located next to the chest wall. Since the intensity of the chest wall is similar to the adjacent nodules in CT scan, it is hard to delineate their boundaries by naked eyes. So, the key issue for segmenting juxta-pleural nodules is to settle the borderline between the nodule and the chest wall. In this paper, a threshold segmentation algorithm based on image transition region and chain code analysis were combined to define the boundary of the nodule. First, the center position and boundary of the nodule were delineated by parsing XML. Then, a 50 × 50 pixels region of interest (ROI) was automatically generated. The segmentation approach was performed on the basis of interactive selection of the 50 × 50 pixels ROI. The workflow chart of the proposed segmentation method is presented in Figure 1A.

Snippet: We next test our proposed framework for lung segmentation of chest radiographs with pulmonary opacities.Lung segmentation of chest radiographs with pulmonary opacities is a challenging task.The presence of pulmonary opacities, such as infections, masses, or consolidations, can introduce significant uncertainty in accurately delineating the lung boundaries.The opacities can obscure the true lung margins, making it difficult to determine the exact extent of the lungs.Due to the ambiguity introduced by the pulmonary opacities, different radiologists or experts may provide varying lung segmentation labels for the same chest radiograph.There can be disagreement on where to draw the precise lung boundaries, especially in regions with opacity.

In this experiment, a collection of chest radiographs with pulmonary opacities are synthesized based on the lung X-ray dataset [3,6] which comprises 640 data-label pairs for training and 63  pairs for testing with the size of (180, 180).To simulate real-world scenarios, we introduce random intensity occlusions to intact the radiographs.The two corresponding segmentation masks labeled by two different experts are generated under different rules.The first-kind label is a segmentation mask from the original dataset, indicating the complete region of the lungs.The second kind differs from the original segmentation by randomly removing part of the opacity area to stimulate the doctors' empirical annotations of the lung masks.Using our proposed framework, our goal is to obtain an optimal DMM that fits the dataset with the labeled segmentation mask, as well as predicts the probability associated with each plausible segmentation result.

In the training process, just as the shape reconstruction task, we still randomly sample a chest radiograph with pulmonary opacities x i from the training set and randomly sample one of its two labels as y k i .Then the distribution of the label space consists of two modes with the same probability of 0.5.

Finally, we obtained the segmentation result by overlapping the extracted foreground with the repaired lung parenchyma mask. Results: To validate the performance of the proposed segmentation approach, we selected 50 juxta-pleural nodules with diameter ranges from 5 mm to 10 mm from Lung Image Database Consortium (LIDC) database. Compared with the ground truth generated by radiologists, we achieved an average overlap rate of 76.93% ± 0.06 with a false positive rate of 13.09% ± 0.09. Conclusion: After comparing and analyzing the segmentation results, we found that our approach outperformed the method reported in other literature. The experimental results demonstrated that our new method is an effective approach to segment small-size juxta-pleural pulmonary nodules accurately.

documents.title: Segmentation Refinement of Small-Size Juxta-Pleural Lung Nodules in CT Scans
documents.snippet: According to the CT images, the juxta-pleural pulmonary nodule, or pleural attached nodule, was located next to the chest wall. Since the intensity of the chest wall is similar to the adjacent nodules in CT scan, it is hard to delineate their boundaries by naked eyes. So, the key issue for segmenting juxta-pleural nodules is to settle the borderline between the nodule and the chest wall. In this paper, a threshold segmentation algorithm based on image transition region and chain code analysis were combined to define the boundary of the nodule. First, the center position and boundary of the nodule were delineated by parsing XML. Then, a 50 × 50 pixels region of interest (ROI) was automatically generated. The segmentation approach was performed on the basis of interactive selection of the 50 × 50 pixels ROI. The workflow chart of the proposed segmentation method is presented in Figure 1A.

documents.title: A deep neural network framework for dynamic multi-valued mapping estimation and its applications
documents.snippet:
We next test our proposed framework for lung segmentation of chest radiographs with pulmonary opacities.Lung segmentation of chest radiographs with pulmonary opacities is a challenging task.The presence of pulmonary opacities, such as infections, masses, or consolidations, can introduce significant uncertainty in accurately delineating the lung boundaries.The opacities can obscure the true lung margins, making it difficult to determine the exact extent of the lungs.Due to the ambiguity introduced by the pulmonary opacities, different radiologists or experts may provide varying lung segmentation labels for the same chest radiograph.There can be disagreement on where to draw the precise lung boundaries, especially in regions with opacity.

In this experiment, a collection of chest radiographs with pulmonary opacities are synthesized based on the lung X-ray dataset [3,6] which comprises 640 data-label pairs for training and 63  pairs for testing with the size of (180, 180).To simulate real-world scenarios, we introduce random intensity occlusions to intact the radiographs.The two corresponding segmentation masks labeled by two different experts are generated under different rules.The first-kind label is a segmentation mask from the original dataset, indicating the complete region of the lungs.The second kind differs from the original segmentation by randomly removing part of the opacity area to stimulate the doctors' empirical annotations of the lung masks.Using our proposed framework, our goal is to obtain an optimal DMM that fits the dataset with the labeled segmentation mask, as well as predicts the probability associated with each plausible segmentation result.

In the training process, just as the shape reconstruction task, we still randomly sample a chest radiograph with pulmonary opacities x i from the training set and randomly sample one of its two labels as y k i .Then the distribution of the label space consists of two modes with the same probability of 0.5.

To show the test results, we output predictions of chest radiograph from the testing set with explicit probability estimates (P (ŷ j i |x i ) > 1e −5 ) annotated on the upper-left corner in the second row in Fig. 6.More results are in Fig. 11.
